World.title: Guadalajara residents turn to citizen science as water crisis deepens
World.content:
On a Saturday morning in Guadalajara’s historic Analco neighborhood, residents arrived at the Casa Bandera community center carrying bottles and jars filled with water from their homes.

At folding tables, researchers from ITESO, Guadalajara’s Jesuit university, showed them how to dip inexpensive reactive strips into the samples, wait for the colors to change and compare the results against a chart measuring pH, chlorine, lead, mercury and other indicators. Samples showing signs of possible bacterial contamination could undergo additional testing for E. coli.

It was the latest workshop in an expanding citizen water-monitoring network that has grown out of Guadalajara’s months-long water crisis — and out of residents’ frustration with what they see as inadequate information and action from the authorities responsible for providing safe water.

“We don’t claim to be scientific specialists or water experts,” Héctor Morales, one of the workshop presenters, told participants. “We are citizens contributing evidence from what we are observing and living through, and that is equally valid.”

“We’re not trying to compete with science,” he continued. “We’re trying to generate knowledge that comes from everyday life. That’s the approach of citizen science.”

Sunday: Mega March + Agua KK Fest

Guadalajara’s water activists will be having some fun with the theme at Sunday’s festival — without losing sight of the very serious problem behind it.

When: Sunday, Aug. 23

10 a.m.: Gather at Parque Rojo

11 a.m.: Mega March for Water departs along Av. Juárez

Noon: Agua KK Fest at Plaza Liberación

The workshops will feature home water filters, rainwater harvesting, dry toilets and water testing, plus children’s activities, music, decorated water jugs, costumes and karaoke. The cheeky Agua KK name is a play on the word caca — a pointed joke about the dirty water that residents say has been coming from their taps.

From complaints to citizen evidence

The network brings together neighborhood residents, scientists from ITESO University, the Mexican Institute for Community Development (IMDEC) and the citizen campaign #ElSiapaQueQueremos, or The SIAPA We Want — SIAPA being the city water utility.

The idea is not simply to tell residents what might be in their water. María González of IMDEC said the testing has two purposes: helping families take care of themselves, and creating a body of evidence that can be used to press authorities for action.

“This helps us protect ourselves. You are going to know what is in the water in your homes,” González told the group. But the results, she said, are also “our citizen evidence for legal action, for institutional action, for mobilization.”

Before Saturday’s workshop, the network had analyzed roughly 184 samples from 90 neighborhoods in five municipalities. Organizers said residual chlorine was found in only 12 of the 184 samples. That’s a problem, they pointed out. Chlorine is added during water treatment, and a small amount should remain as water travels through the distribution network to help protect it from bacterial contamination.

The monitoring also detected lead in 20 samples, fluoride in 52 and mercury in an unspecified number, according to Morales. Four of the 184 samples tested positive for E. coli, a form of fecal coliform bacteria.

The citizen findings are not a statistically representative survey of Guadalajara’s water supply, a limitation organizers repeatedly emphasized. The low-cost tests do not measure all of the dozens of parameters required under Mexico’s drinking-water standard.

“What does this analysis tell us?” Morales asked. “It tells us when the water is not safe. What doesn’t it tell us? It doesn’t tell us when the water is good.”

Certifying water as safe, he said, requires much more extensive laboratory testing.

Still, official testing has now documented some of the same warning signs.

In late July, Jalisco health authorities confirmed that E. coli had been detected in 18 of 297 samples analyzed between March and June in neighborhoods affected by water-quality problems. Officials also acknowledged insufficient chlorination in some areas.

The findings came after months of complaints about yellow, brown or foul-smelling water, as well as sediment and service interruptions across the Guadalajara metropolitan area. González said the #ElSiapaQueQueremos campaign has now received nearly 1,500 complaints, with water quality by far the most common problem, followed by outages and high rates.

A multibillion-peso response

The Jalisco government and SIAPA, the metropolitan water utility, have acknowledged serious problems in the aging system and announced a long-term overhaul requiring more than 20 billion pesos in investment.

Among the major projects are the replacement of the aging Chapala-Guadalajara aqueduct and the modernization and expansion of Potabilizadora No. 1 in Miravalle. Governor Pablo Lemus said this month that the federal government had agreed to support both projects.

But for the citizen coalition, repairing infrastructure is only part of the solution.

The movement is increasingly focusing on who participates in decisions about the water system, how information is shared and whether communities themselves can have a formal role in monitoring and oversight.

That shift will be on display Sunday, when the same groups organizing the monitoring workshops will hold a “Mega March for Water.” Participants will gather at Parque Rojo at 10 a.m. and march along Avenida Juárez to Plaza Liberación, where the deliberately scatological “Agua KK Fest” — a play on caca, or “poop,” in reference to residents’ complaints about dirty water — will begin at noon.

The festival will combine protest with workshops on household filters, rainwater harvesting, dry toilets, urban gardens, community water systems and water-quality monitoring. Organizers describe the event as peaceful, family-oriented and nonpartisan.

Beyond fixing SIAPA

The coalition’s demands now extend beyond cleaner water. Its latest statement calls for greater transparency, citizen participation in decisions over water quality, distribution and infrastructure, formal recognition of community monitoring and protection of the watersheds that supply the metropolitan area.

It also proposes “public-community agreements” that would bring SIAPA, universities, neighborhood organizations, workers and other sectors together to share knowledge and participate in water governance.

The organizers explicitly reject privatization as the answer to SIAPA’s failures.

“The alternative to an inefficient SIAPA is not a privatized SIAPA,” their statement says, calling instead for a public utility that is transparent, efficient and subject to democratic social oversight.

González said the campaign is also pushing for a permanent working group focused specifically on water quality, health and sanitary risks. Authorities have not yet agreed to participate.

But organizers do not intend to wait indefinitely.

The group, González said, “is going to be established with authorities or without authorities,” functioning independently if necessary to prevent health risks.

That determination reflects how far the movement has come since residents first began showing up at public meetings with bottles of discolored water.

Morales said citizen monitoring allows residents to reach places government agencies may not sample and to turn individual experiences into systematic evidence. He has watched workshop participants take what they learn back to their neighborhoods — and then into the streets.

“It’s beautiful to see people who come to the workshops later at demonstrations with signs saying, ‘There are nitrates and nitrites in our water,’” he said.

“The authorities never expected that.”

World.title: The story of Zarzaparilla, an Indigenous root beer from Veracruz
World.content:
Mexico’s truest beauty can often be found in its widely diverse, uniquely regional variations of culture and flavors. No two places in Mexico are exactly alike. Whether it’s the way a certain salsa is prepared, the protein of choice used to stuff a tamal or the techniques that may differ from coast to coast, pueblo to pueblo, the country reflects an endless multiverse of realities inside its kitchens. As a taxi driver in Oaxaca once told me while driving across the desert terrain, you can spend two lifetimes in Mexico and even then, you still wouldn’t uncover all of its secrets and taste all of its idiosyncrasies.

It was a revelation, then, when I learned about zarzaparilla — about its historic origins and regional importance — from one of my uncles who grew up in Veracruz. In the simplest terms, zarzaparilla (referred to simply as zarza by locals) is what modern consumers would likely associate with root beer. But centuries before making its way into European markets via the Spanish — who in the 16th century first encountered the Indigenous remedy in the mountains of what is now Veracruz, and then exported it to Seville, Spain — zarza was a native drink with purported medicinal qualities made from local roots and ingredients that combated syphilis and, according to the American Homebrewers Association, far predates root beer.

A root beer revelation

In an effort to learn more about it, I drove 45 minutes to the source, on a southbound road from my home in Veracruz past two Pueblos Mágicos — first Coatepec, then Xico — until I reached Mexico’s cradle of zarza: Teocelo (or, in Nahuatl, “Tiger God”).

The mountain town of around 11,000 can only be reached through narrow, curving roads that carve through the subtropical terrain at a high elevation — with humid and wet conditions that allow all sorts of vegetation and crops to flourish in the surrounding areas (coffee, in particular, is a notable product from this part of Mexico).

It’s here that zarzaparilla (also confusingly spelled “sarsaparilla”) gained notoriety as a beverage among Spaniards and mestizos, becoming a local commercial industry of sorts that would expand beyond the region. Today, zarzaparilla can be found throughout Mexico, particularly within Veracruz and its neighboring states. But back then, it was — much like jalapeños were until they became commonplace elsewhere — a specialty product known only to those in the greater Xalapa vicinity.

The origins of ‘zarza’

In snooping around the tiny pueblo, it’s easy to find where it all started: Zarzaparilla Flores (a family-owned business that is not to be mistaken for a separate branch of family operations, Zarzaparilla Flores Doña Chabe, which is literally next door, but technically unaffiliated). The original Zarzaparilla Flores is said to have opened in 1920 inside what used to be a storage building for the nearby train yard, which served as a prominent trade route during the Porfiriato era from Xico to the United States. Due to the train, lots of immigrants and outsiders were able to pass through town, bringing a transient mixture of passersby who helped give zarzaparilla its fame beyond Veracruz.

Today, a third-generation family member runs the business — with antique family photos dating back to the Mexican Revolution bedecking the walls (one photo of the original shop owner, Don Manuel Flores, and his wife hangs stoically beneath two old rifles).

Rubén Olivares is the current face of operations. He married into the Flores family and has taken over the zarzaparilla tradition with pride.

A family tradition and recipe

“This region used to be known for cultivating pineapples and oranges, and that created a local exporting economy early on,” Olivares says. “But over time, with climate change and different farming methods, everything shifted, and pineapple exports migrated further south, due to the hotter temperatures down there. And this area, which has always been colder and at higher altitudes, began to grow coffee and other ingredients that were good for making zarzaparilla.”

Without revealing the specifics of their family recipe, he tells me their zarzaparilla is a mix of ginger, cardamom, star anise, cinnamon, lime, jamaica, egg whites and more. They also sell hidromiel (mead) and other liquors made from fermented oranges, arrowhead plants, cherry and crucetillo (a shrub that in the past was used to treat venomous snakebites).

The family’s zarza recipe has remained the same for more than a century and was patented in 1920 by Don Manuel Flores, but according to Olivares, Don Manuel only sold a few liters of it at the time. The family now regularly brews batches of around 1,000 liters and ships it all over Mexico. Predominantly made as a syrupy concentrate, the molasses-like mixture is put into various sizes of plastic bottles and jugs, which consumers can mix with any ratio of filtered or mineral water to their liking.

How the drink conquered the ‘Wild West’

In the 19th and 20th centuries, the beverage was viewed as a medicinal remedy and was brought to the U.S. According to The Seattle Times, “Sarsaparilla was widely consumed all across 19th-century America, easy to find in the local saloon if the one-road town one rode into had no dedicated apothecary or pharmacy, and was supposedly quite popular with cowboys and ranchers looking to tame a rumbling tummy or put a little pep in their step, much as people use kombucha today.” Eventually — and it’s unclear when, why or how — zarzaparilla (made from “dried root bark of several plants in the genus Smilax,” which grew plentifully in Veracruz) was replaced by sassafras, and zarzaparilla became known as root beer. (In 1960, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration banned real sassafras in commercial root beer as safrole in high amounts was found to be carcinogenic.)

Throughout it all, zarza remained the dominant beverage of choice in and around the town of its origin in Veracruz. The Flores family is no longer the only one making it, either: A Google Maps search will reveal no fewer than five other zarzaparilla businesses in the town of about 23 square miles (for comparison’s sake, Mexico City is estimated at 573 square miles, yet according to Google, unfortunately has no official zarzaparilla-dedicated outlets).

Travel attractions in Teocelo

Teocelo has other worthwhile features besides zarza: It’s the site of the Fiesta Patronal, a weekend-long celebration that includes parades, fireworks and religious celebrations in honor of the burial of Jesus after his crucifixion. At the pueblo’s main entrance, there’s a bee sanctuary that produces all kinds of honey products you likely won’t find anywhere else, at least not in abundance — jugs of honey wine, salsa macha made with honey and “honey butter” (akin to peanut butter, with a similarly thick consistency) in variations that range from almond and walnut to berry or garlic.

Note: The honey shop, known as La Mielada, or “The Honeydew,” also has an accompanying restaurant that serves honeyed meats and breads, with an affordable selection of beverages like the aforementioned honey wine or my personal favorite, a mug of locally cultivated coffee with large dollops of organic honey mixed in — a pure delight of sweet and bitter flavors. For outdoor-seeking adventurers, the surrounding area also offers waterfalls, hikes, cabins and whitewater rapids.

To be sure, there’s no shortage of offerings — and mugs of zarza — to enjoy for a weekend in the chilly mountain locale.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: The hottest product on the planet is increasingly made in Mexico: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Let’s start today’s column with a quick quiz:

Pop Quiz Question #1: What is currently the top Mexican export to the United States?

If you are like most people, you are thinking of one of three categories: alcoholic beverages (think tequila, mezcal, Corona beer), food (perhaps avocados, jalapenos, tomatoes) or automobiles. All of those answers are incorrect.

Pop Quiz Question #2: Which country sells more AI servers and equipment to the United States, Mexico or Taiwan?

Of course, most people answer Taiwan. That would also be incorrect.

Mexico’s server-related exports to the US have overtaken autos, underscoring how AI data-center demand is reshaping its export base. Source: @financialtimes https://t.co/QtrH6mKZ0I pic.twitter.com/pyRYc40ktb — (((The Daily Shot))) (@SoberLook) August 7, 2026

Sometimes just one picture, or in this case — one chart recently published by the Financial Times — can be incredibly insightful. Above, you’ll see a chart comparing Mexican exports of two product categories from 2010 to the present day. The blue line shows vehicles, which Mexico has been exporting for over 60 years. Last year, nearly 80% of Mexico’s light vehicle exports went to the United States. The red line shows server-related hardware (think AI data centers). The x-axis shows the years from 2010 to 2026. The y-axis shows monthly exports in billions of US dollars.

As can be clearly seen, exports of server-related hardware have absolutely exploded in the past two years, to the point where they are now surpassing vehicles. Last month alone, over US $15 billion of these products were exported. Think about that for a minute. The news is filled on a daily basis with headlines telling us that Trump has decided not to renew the USMCA or that Trump commented that “we don’t need anything that Mexico has.” Other headlines lead us to believe that tariffs are being slapped on most Mexican goods, significantly hurting Mexico in the process. Neither is true.

That being said, much of the conversation often seems to revolve around two categories of products highly influenced by two distinct voting groups in the U.S. The first is union members and more specifically the members of the United Auto Workers, who have an obvious interest in keeping as much vehicle production as possible in the country. The second is U.S. farmers, who naturally want to keep food production domestic. As a result of these two powerful and influential groups, those segments are what we most often hear about — more specifically cars and tomatoes. And in fact, the U.S. currently has a 17% “antidumping” tariff on Mexican tomatoes and a relatively small and extremely complex-to-calculate tariff on Mexican vehicles. Fun fact: One of the final projects my senior year of college was to analyze the impact of U.S. tomato tariff practices and policies on Mexico. (Yes, I am aware of what an exceptionally boring topic that is for a final project!)

Perhaps not surprisingly, server equipment from Mexico has a 0% tariff from the United States. The most in-demand product on the planet right now has firmly established Mexico in its supply chain, and investment, jobs and exports are all booming in this area. Taiwanese companies are investing heavily in Mexico. It’s all happening very fast. It’s quite exciting and going to be very interesting to continue to follow.

So while most headlines would have you believe that the Mexico-U.S. trade relationship is in shambles, the reality is as follows:

1. Mexico moves past Taiwan as the top AI server exporter to the U.S.: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/business/mexico-moves-past-taiwan-as-top-ai-server-exporter-to-united-states/

2. Mexico is now by far the leading exporter to the U.S.: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/business/mexico-in-numbers-mexico-exports-us-china-canada/

3. Inflation is now lower in Mexico than in the U.S. for the first time: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/business/inflation-mexico-lower-united-states-why-thats-such-a-big-deal-a-perspective-from-our-ceo/

4. Mexico’s export revenue is up 25% so far this year: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/news/mexico-export-revenue-this-year/

So what’s the bottom line here? Follow the data, not the noise, and stay tuned to what is the most dynamic segment in the world, growing fast and furious right here in Mexico.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Missed the deadline? Here’s how to get your cell phone service back
World.content:
The first enforced deadline for compliance with mandatory cell phone registration came and went on Aug. 15 and approximately 2.6 million phone lines were suspended, prompting chaos and confusion for users whose now-unregistered phone numbers end in “0.”

Mexico’s Telecommunications Regulatory Commission (CRT) announced on Thursday that nearly 9.7 million users whose number ends in “0” successfully registered their cell phones before the deadline.

The CRT also said that just over 2.3 million users whose lines had been suspended managed to reactivate their phone service by Aug. 19. Another 2.6 million mobile phones are expected to be reactivated in the coming days, while the CRT expects 2.5 million “unused” lines to be decommissioned.

Those who failed to register before the deadline faced plenty of online misinformation, but those whose service was suspended can still recover their service because their phone number was not canceled.

To reactivate the service, users must complete the registration process via their phone company. Prepaid lines must also be registered to remain active.

You can register through the phone company’s registration portal and by verifying your identity. Links to all providers’ platforms can be found on the CRT website here.

You can also complete the process in person at one of your company’s customer service centers, where staff is on hand to assist with the registration.

Mexican mobile phone owners must provide a CURP (Unique Population Registry Code) and a valid official ID, such as the INE-issued voter ID.

Foreigners must also register their phone lines (if it is a Mexican provider) by using the corresponding identity or immigration document, such as a resident visa or a passport.

Procedures vary slightly depending on the phone company, but the process is free.

It is important to note that suspended lines can still make calls to emergency numbers, citizen services and their phone company. They will also continue to receive earthquake alerts and they can be used to complete the registration process.

The government mandated cell phone registration procedures in an effort to eliminate anonymous mobile lines, stop criminal extortion and curb the use of untraceable “burner” prepaid SIM cards.

The CRT had originally established a June 30 deadline for all cell phones to be registered, but when it became apparent that a significant number of users would see their lines suspended, the deadline was extended.

The official schedule to register cell phones now depends on the final digit of your phone number. If your phone number ends in “1,” you must register by Aug. 31. If it ends in “2,” your deadline is Sept. 15, and so on through the end of the year as shown in the graphic above.

In its Aug. 20 report, the CRT said a total of 73.2 million lines — or 60.5% of the total lines expected to be connected in the country — were registered. By the end of the registration process, it expects a purge of around 25 million lines.

With reports from El Universal, Wired and LatinUS

World.title: Ecuador Cocaine Seizure at Posorja Port Was Bound for Mexico
World.content:
Ecuador · SECURITY

Key Facts — Seizure 1.01 tonnes of cocaine, a gross weight of 1,011.52 kilograms, found on 21 August 2026

— Where The Posorja deep-water port in Guayas province, on Ecuador’s Pacific coast

— Hidden 928 blocks packed inside the structures of four machines in a single container

— Destination The Mexican Pacific port of Lázaro Cárdenas, in the state of Michoacán

— Value US$2.1 million in Ecuador, US$27.7 million in the United States, US$43.17 million in Europe

A risk-analysis unit had flagged the container eight days earlier. When police finally opened it, the cocaine was inside the machinery itself.

Officers of Ecuador’s National Police in Durán, Guayas province, in 2024. The force seized 1.01 tonnes of cocaine at Posorja on 21 August 2026.

An Ecuador cocaine seizure at the port of Posorja stopped 1.01 tonnes of the drug on Friday 21 August 2026. The container had been declared as machinery, and it was booked for Mexico, the Ministry of the Interior said.

Inside the Ecuador Cocaine Seizure

The Ecuador cocaine seizure happened at the deep-water port of Posorja, in the coastal province of Guayas. The ministry gave the gross weight as 1,011.52 kilograms.

That is about 9.23 million doses, according to the same bulletin. In short, it is a large shipment even by the standards of Ecuador’s docks.

The ministry published its account the same day, 21 August 2026. It set out the weight, the packaging and where the box was going.

A Container Declared as Machinery

The cocaine was packed into 928 blocks. Those blocks were hidden inside the structures of four machines, all loaded into one container.

On paper, the box was carrying an electromagnetic lifting system, in Spanish a sistema electromagnético de elevación. Because the drug sat inside the metal itself, a quick look at the cargo would have shown nothing.

A deep-water port can take the largest container ships without constant dredging. Posorja therefore loads vessels that cannot reach the river terminals at Guayaquil.

How Risk Analysis Flagged the Box

The case did not begin at the quayside. It began on 13 August 2026, when a unit called CIAPA marked the container as risky and ordered it blocked.

CIAPA is the Centro Integrado de Análisis de Puertos y Aeropuertos, the joint centre that profiles port and airport cargo. After that block, officers opened the container and found the blocks inside the machines.

Cargo profiling means checking a shipment’s paperwork, route and history before anyone opens it. Here the flag came eight days before the seizure was announced.

Once a container is blocked, it cannot be loaded onto a ship. It stays in the terminal until officers open it and either clear or seize the cargo.

Who Ran the Operation

The ministry named the operation FÉNIX-0438, Encuentro 117. The National Police carried it out with the Fiscalía General del Estado, Ecuador’s state prosecution service.

John Reimberg, the interior minister, announced the result. However, the bulletin reported no arrests, and it described the cargo and the destination instead.

The Fiscalía General del Estado is Ecuador’s public prosecution service. It works with the police from the start of a criminal case.

What the Cargo Was Worth

The ministry gave three values for the same cocaine. It put the load at US$2.1 million in Ecuador, US$27.7 million in the United States and US$43.17 million in Europe.

The gap is the whole business model of the route. As a result, a container that never leaves the Pacific coast is worth a fraction of what it fetches in Europe.

The three figures describe three markets, not three separate loads. On the ministry’s own numbers, the cocaine is worth about twenty times more in Europe than in Ecuador.

Why Posorja Matters

Posorja is a rural parish in Guayas, the province that also holds Guayaquil, Ecuador’s biggest city. Its deep-water terminal is run by DP World and opened in August 2019.

Since then it has grown quickly. In April 2026, DP World inaugurated a 700-metre quay extension.

That lifted capacity from about 1 million to 1.4 million TEU a year. Guayaquil is Ecuador’s largest city and its commercial centre.

Its terminals sit on the Guayas river, while Posorja lies closer to open water. More boxes also mean more cover for a smuggler.

In 2025, the terminal recorded the largest single share of cocaine found at Ecuadorean ports.

Scanners at Every Export Port

TEU means twenty-foot equivalent unit, the standard way of counting shipping containers. Since 2024, Ecuador has scanned 100 percent of the export cargo leaving its ports.

Even so, the pressure has not eased. A World Customs Organization report looked at cocaine found in shipping containers worldwide.

Of that total, 385 tonnes, or 30 percent, had a declared loading port in Ecuador. Scanning every export box still leaves the images to be read by people.

In this case the container was flagged by paperwork and risk data, not by a scanner. That 385 tonnes is what customs services detected, not what was shipped.

In other words, it is the share the checks managed to catch.

Where the Container Was Heading

The declared destination was Lázaro Cárdenas, on Mexico’s Pacific coast in the state of Michoacán. Along with Manzanillo in Colima, it is one of the main Mexican ports where drugs shipped from South America arrive.

This load never got there. Before the ship sailed, the container was blocked, opened and emptied in Ecuador.

Michoacán sits on Mexico’s Pacific coast. Manzanillo, further north along the same coast, receives the same kind of traffic.

A Year of Big Busts

The Posorja case is not unusual. For example, 1.6 tonnes were seized near the Colombian border on 12 August 2026.

Three days earlier, 1.2 tonnes bound for Spain turned up in boxes of fruit. Earlier in the summer, 1.2 tonnes bound for Latvia were seized on 26 July.

Before that, more than 1.5 tonnes turned up in a fruit container booked for Denmark on 12 July. Ecuador’s National Police reported 222.37 tonnes of drugs seized between 1 January and 29 December 2025.

A wider government count put the year at 214.53 tonnes, against 294.61 tonnes in 2024.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was seized at Posorja port?

Police found 1.01 tonnes of cocaine, a gross weight of 1,011.52 kilograms. It was packed in 928 blocks hidden inside four machines in one container.

Where was the container going?

Its declared destination was Lázaro Cárdenas, a Pacific port in the Mexican state of Michoacán. The container never left Ecuador.

How was the shipment found?

A cargo profiling unit known as CIAPA flagged the container as risky on 13 August 2026 and had it blocked. Officers then opened it and found the drug.

Was anyone arrested?

The Interior Ministry’s bulletin reported no arrests in this operation. It set out the weight, the hiding place and the destination instead.

Sources: Ecuador’s Ministry of the Interior; Primicias; El Universo; Expreso; Infobae.

World.title: O Globo Just Named São Paulo’s Best Varied-Cuisine Restaurants
World.content:
BRAZIL · FOOD

Key Facts Who publishes it O Globo, through its SP Gastronomia section and award.

O Globo, through its SP Gastronomia section and award. Published 21 August 2026, updated the following day.

21 August 2026, updated the following day. Size Around 300 addresses across the city, in several categories.

Around 300 addresses across the city, in several categories. This list Cozinha variada, meaning kitchens that do not sit in one national tradition.

Main courses run from about R$69 to R$320, or US$13 to US$62. Note Several entries have two or more addresses in different neighbourhoods.

About 300 addresses, one useful category, and prices you can actually plan around.

The Guia SP Gastronomia 2026 was published on 21 August. Its varied-cuisine list is the most useful section for anyone who does not already know the city.

Arturito, in Jardim Paulista, is one of the varied-cuisine picks.

What the guide is

The Guia SP Gastronomia is published by O Globo, the Rio newspaper, through a dedicated São Paulo food section.

The 2026 edition covers roughly 300 addresses. It includes restaurants, bakeries, patisseries and ice cream shops.

It is organised by category rather than by ranking. Cozinha variada sits alongside Latin American, Greek, Jewish and Scandinavian sections.

The category articles were published on 21 August 2026. The main award piece was updated the next day.

It functions the way a city guide should. It is a curated list, not a competition with one winner.

O Globo has run the São Paulo guide for years. The paulistano trade treats it as a fixed point in the calendar.

What cozinha variada actually means

The term does not translate cleanly. It means a kitchen that does not belong to a single national tradition.

In practice these are the restaurants a paulistano recommends when a visitor has no fixed idea what they want.

That makes it the most useful category in the Guia SP Gastronomia for a newcomer to the city.

You are not committing to Italian, Japanese or Brazilian. You are committing to a kitchen.

The selection spans roughly R$69 to R$320 for a main course, so it is not a single price bracket.

Categories like Greek, Jewish and Scandinavian sit alongside it, each with its own short list.

The established names

Carlota has occupied a white house in Higienópolis since 1995, under Carla Pernambuco. Its beef wellington runs R$155.

Bistrô Charlô dates from 1988 and stays firmly French. The foie gras terrine is R$220 and the filet rossini R$320.

Spot, on Alameda Ministro Rocha Azevedo in Bela Vista, has been busy since 1994. Main courses sit around R$99 to R$135.

A Figueira Rubaiyat in Jardins is built around a hundred-year-old fig tree that grows through the glass roof.

Its weekday set lunch, with starter, a cut of beef, side and dessert, is R$151, about US$29.

Prices below are as published by the guide and will move with the menu.

The newer rooms

Caco opened in early 2025 in Pinheiros, in a white brick townhouse. Pasta courses run R$77 to R$79.

Lita, also in Pinheiros, is the newest venture from chef Tássia Magalhães and sommelier Danyel Steinle.

Its wine list carries more than 400 labels, with vermouth on tap. Small sharing plates start around R$38.

Motel, in Consolação, belongs to Renata Vanzetto’s group and is deliberately provocative in decor and menu.

Reserve or arrive early there. It has been full since it opened.

Newer rooms tend to be smaller, which makes booking more important than at the older houses.

Where the value is

Several entries run weekday set menus that cost a fraction of the a la carte prices.

Esther Rooftop in República offers starter, main and dessert for R$97, about US$19, with a view over the centre.

Nou in Pinheiros runs an executive lunch between R$64 and R$74, with four main courses to choose from.

Carlota’s weekday menu formula is R$98 for three courses. Mescla in Barra Funda does one for R$59.

Rascal, with ten São Paulo branches, is all-you-can-eat at R$128 to R$144 depending on day and location.

Weekday lunch is where the gap between local and visitor pricing is widest.

The ones with a view or a room

Skye sits on the top floor of the Unique hotel, looking over Avenida Paulista and Ibirapuera Park.

Its kitchen is led by Emmanuel Bassoleil. Main courses run R$155 to R$165, or US$30 to US$32.

Esther Rooftop occupies the top of a modernist landmark building in the centre.

Holy Tavern in Vila Buarque has 23 seats and requires a reservation. It opens only in the evening.

Borgo Mooca, despite the name, is in Santa Cecilia and has a cocktail bar in its basement.

A rooftop table in São Paulo needs booking in the dry season, which is now.

Reading a São Paulo menu price

Prices in the Guia SP Gastronomia are quoted in Brazilian reais, and they move.

At the PTAX selling rate of 5.1625 reais to the dollar for 21 August 2026, R$100 is about US$19.

That puts a R$155 main course at roughly US$30 and a R$59 set lunch at about US$11.

Set lunches are where São Paulo is genuinely cheap relative to comparable cities.

Dinner at the top of this list is not cheap by any measure, local or foreign.

Card payment is universal at this level, and a service charge of ten per cent is normal.

How to use the list

Do not try to work through it. Around 300 addresses is a reference, not an itinerary.

Pick by neighbourhood first. Pinheiros, Jardins, Higienópolis and Itaim carry most of the selection.

Check opening hours before travelling. Many of these close on Mondays or open only for lunch.

Reserve for the small rooms. Holy Tavern, Nomo and Motel all fill.

The Guia SP Gastronomia also runs Bom e Barato, a cheaper parallel list worth reading alongside this one.

The Guia SP Gastronomia is in Portuguese only, so a browser translation is worth having open.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who publishes the Guia SP Gastronomia? O Globo, through its SP Gastronomia section. The 2026 category lists were published on 21 August 2026. What does cozinha variada mean? Varied cuisine. Kitchens that do not sit inside a single national tradition, which makes it the most useful category for a newcomer. How expensive is it? Main courses across the selection run about R$69 to R$320. That is roughly US$13 to US$62 at the PTAX selling rate of 5.1625 for 21 August 2026. Is there a cheaper option? Yes. Several entries run weekday set menus from R$59 to R$98, and the guide has a separate Bom e Barato list. How many restaurants are in the guide? Around 300 addresses in total across all categories, including bakeries and ice cream shops.

World.title: A García Márquez Novel Becomes a One-Man Show in Barranco
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

PERU · THEATRE

Key Facts — What En los Tiempos del Cólera, a one-person staged narration.

— Based on El amor en los tiempos del cólera, the 1985 García Márquez novel.

— When Saturday 29 August 2026 at 6pm.

— Where La Vermut Bar, Avenida Bolognesi 235, Barranco, Lima.

— Price Not published, so ask the venue before travelling.

— Format Narración oral escénica, closer to storytelling than to conventional theatre.

One actor, one novel, one small room in Lima’s most walkable district.

A stage version of García Márquez’s Love in the Time of Cholera plays in Barranco on Saturday 29 August. It runs as a one-person spoken performance.

La Vermut Bar sits a few streets inland from this bridge.

What is being staged

The piece is called En los Tiempos del Cólera. It is billed as a narración oral escénica.

That form sits between theatre and storytelling. One performer holds the room without a set or a cast.

The source is El amor en los tiempos del cólera, the novel García Márquez published in 1985. The English title is Love in the Time of Cholera.

It is his most widely read book after One Hundred Years of Solitude. This is García Márquez in Barranco stripped to its simplest possible staging.

García Márquez in Barranco is a single date, not a run, which is worth knowing before you plan around it.

When and where

The performance is on Saturday 29 August 2026. It begins at 6pm.

The venue is La Vermut Bar, at Avenida Bolognesi 235 in Barranco, Lima. Bolognesi is one of the district’s main avenues, walkable from the centre of Barranco.

A bar rather than a theatre changes the evening. Expect to be close and to have a drink in hand.

The listing gives one date only. There is no announced season.

La Vermut Bar is a small room, so the 6pm start is likely to be kept.

What is not published

The ticket price has not been published anywhere we can find. Neither has the booking method.

There is no Teleticket or Joinnus link in the listing. That usually means door sales or a reservation by message.

No capacity figure is given either. A bar room of this kind seats tens, not hundreds.

The performer and adaptor are named in the event card but not in a way we can verify independently. The practical answer is to contact La Vermut Bar directly before making the trip.

Venues of this size in Lima often take reservations by WhatsApp rather than through a ticketing site.

Why this novel

Love in the Time of Cholera is a love story that runs across fifty-one years, nine months and four days. Florentino Ariza waits that long for Fermina Daza.

The novel treats the wait as neither noble nor absurd. It is set on Colombia’s Caribbean coast, in an unnamed city drawn from Cartagena.

The book is less fantastical than One Hundred Years of Solitude. Its magic is in the patience.

That makes it unusually suited to one voice in one room. The novel drew on his own parents’ courtship, which he described as the seed of the book.

What a narración oral escénica is

The form is well established across Latin America and barely known elsewhere. A single narrator performs a text rather than acting a character.

The audience is addressed directly. There is no fourth wall and usually no set.

The whole thing rests on timing and voice. It is the closest live equivalent to being read to as an adult.

For anyone with intermediate Spanish it is easier to follow than ensemble theatre. Peru has a strong tradition in the form, with festivals dedicated to it in Lima and Cusco.

Barranco itself

Barranco is Lima’s smallest and most walkable district, on the cliffs south of Miraflores. It has the highest concentration of bars, galleries and small venues in the city.

The district was a seaside resort for Lima’s wealthy in the nineteenth century. The architecture still shows it.

Most visitors come for the Puente de los Suspiros and stay for the evening. García Márquez in Barranco fits the district exactly.

Small rooms, literary crowd, no formality. García Márquez in Barranco sits within a few streets of a dozen other small venues.

Getting there

Barranco is about twenty minutes from Miraflores by taxi and longer in traffic. Ride apps work normally throughout the district.

Street taxis are best avoided. The Metropolitano bus runs along the Via Expresa with stops within walking distance.

Avenida Bolognesi runs inland from the seafront, so the address is a short walk from the main square. A 6pm start means arriving in daylight, which makes the walk straightforward.

Barranco fills on Saturday evenings, so allow extra time for the last few blocks.

Is it worth the evening

For anyone who reads Spanish comfortably, this is an easy recommendation. For anyone still learning, a narrated performance is gentler than a play with several speakers.

The unpublished price is the one real obstacle. Ask first.

One date only means there is no second chance if you miss it. García Márquez in Barranco on a Saturday evening is a small, specific pleasure.

That is the whole appeal. Bring cash.

Small Barranco bars do not always take foreign cards.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is García Márquez in Barranco being staged? On Saturday 29 August 2026 at 6pm, at La Vermut Bar in Barranco, Lima. What is the address? La Vermut Bar, Avenida Bolognesi 235, Barranco, Lima. How much does it cost? The price has not been published. Contact the venue directly before travelling. Which novel is it based on? El amor en los tiempos del cólera, published in 1985 and known in English as Love in the Time of Cholera. Is it in Spanish? Yes. It is a one-person narrated performance, which is easier to follow than ensemble theatre if your Spanish is intermediate.

Uruguay · FINANCE

Key Facts — Portfolio size CAF’s Uruguay portfolio has doubled to about US$2 billion.

— Timeframe The doubling occurred over the last five years.

— Water project CAF funds a US$200 million dam project on the Casupá stream.

— Meeting CAF will host economy ministers in Montevideo on 1 October 2026.

— Membership CAF has 25 member countries.

The regional lender is expanding its footprint in Uruguay, with a focus on water security and infrastructure projects.

Has doubled its CAF portfolio in Uruguay to about US$2 billion, according to El Observador. CAF, the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean.

The portfolio now includes credits and projects that support infrastructure and development across the country.

CAF Portfolio Growth in Uruguay

The CAF portfolio in Uruguay has grown steadily over the last five years, reaching roughly US$2 billion. This expansion reflects the bank’s commitment to financing long-term public works in the region.

According to El Observador, the portfolio consists of credits and projects that benefit local communities. In addition, the bank focuses on sustainable infrastructure and climate resilience.

Water Security and Infrastructure Focus

A key part of the CAF portfolio involves water security and drinking water infrastructure. For example, CAF funds a US$200 million project to build a dam on the Casupá stream.

This dam is designed to secure water supply for the Montevideo metropolitan area. Moreover, the bank also finances roads, power, and water projects as part of regional infrastructure packages.

Upcoming Montevideo Meeting

CAF will host a meeting of economy ministers and delegations from its 25 member countries in Montevideo on 1 October 2026. This meeting coincides with Uruguay holding the presidency of CAF’s governing body.

At the meeting, ministers and delegations will approve new credit operations and technical assistance instruments for the region. Therefore, the event marks a significant moment for regional cooperation.

Role of a Multilateral Development Bank

CAF is a multilateral development bank, which means it is owned by governments. These banks lend to governments at better terms than private markets, usually for long-term public works.

As a result, CAF finances sustainable infrastructure, climate resilience, water and sanitation, energy transition, productivity, and urban mobility. This broad mandate helps countries like Uruguay address pressing development needs.

Impact on Infrastructure Projects

The CAF portfolio supports a variety of infrastructure projects that improve daily life. For instance, water security projects ensure reliable drinking water for growing urban areas.

Meanwhile, road and power projects enhance connectivity and energy access. Overall, these investments contribute to economic growth and social well-being.

Regional Cooperation and Development

By doubling its CAF portfolio in Uruguay, the bank demonstrates its role in fostering regional development. Moreover, the upcoming meeting in Montevideo highlights the importance of collective action among member countries.

Since Uruguay holds the presidency of CAF’s governing body, it plays a central role in shaping the bank’s agenda. Consequently, this meeting will likely strengthen ties among Latin American and Caribbean nations.

Future Prospects for Uruguay

With the expanded CAF portfolio, Uruguay can pursue more ambitious infrastructure goals. For example, the dam project on the Casupá stream will secure water supply for years to come.

In addition, new credit operations approved at the October meeting could unlock further investments. Therefore, the future looks promising for Uruguay’s development trajectory.

Commitment to Sustainable Development

CAF’s portfolio emphasizes sustainability and climate resilience. This approach aligns with global efforts to address environmental challenges.

By financing water, energy, and mobility projects, the bank helps countries transition to more sustainable models. In short, the CAF portfolio is a tool for positive change.

Conclusion: A Growing Partnership

In conclusion, the doubling of the CAF portfolio in Uruguay signifies a deepening partnership. The bank’s investments in water security and infrastructure will have lasting benefits.

As the October meeting approaches, anticipation builds for new approvals that could further expand the CAF portfolio. Overall, this collaboration bodes well for Uruguay’s future.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the CAF portfolio in Uruguay?

The CAF portfolio in Uruguay refers to the credits and projects financed by CAF. The Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean.

What types of projects does CAF finance in Uruguay?

CAF finances infrastructure and development operations, including water security and drinking water infrastructure. It also supports roads, power, and water projects.

When is CAF’s meeting in Montevideo?

CAF will host a meeting of economy ministers and delegations from its 25 member countries in Montevideo on 1 October 2026. The meeting will approve new credit operations and technical assistance instruments.

How does CAF benefit Uruguay?

CAF provides funding at better terms than private markets, which helps Uruguay finance long-term public works. This includes projects like the US$200 million dam on the Casupá stream.

Sources: El Observador; CAF; BNamericas.

The waiver follows a six-month payment pause for homeowners hit by Hurricane Melissa, easing costs for about 36,000 mortgages.

The National Housing Trust has waived J$585 million in storm insurance premiums for Jamaican homeowners. Prime Minister Andrew Holness announced the move on 6 June 2026.

And the Jamaica Gleaner and Caribbean News Global reported on it again in August.

What the Waiver Covers

The National Housing Trust waived peril-insurance costs for mortgage holders who benefited from a six-month moratorium. This pause ran from November 2025 to April 2026, following Hurricane Melissa.

Peril insurance on an NHT mortgage covers damage from events like hurricanes. It is normally compulsory, and the premium is charged to the borrower.

Who Benefits

About 36,000 mortgages in affected areas received the six-month moratorium. State minister Fitz-Henley gave this figure in Parliament, reported on 6 June 2026.

Therefore, the waiver applies to those same mortgage holders.

Understanding the Moratorium

A moratorium is a pause on payments. It does not cancel the debt, but it stops instalments falling due for a set period.

In this case, the pause helped homeowners recover from the storm. Meanwhile, the premium waiver removes an additional financial burden.

The Role of the National Housing Trust

The National Housing Trust is Jamaica’s state housing agency. It is funded by contributions from workers and employers and lends for home purchase and construction.

As a result, the trust plays a key role in helping Jamaicans own homes. This waiver is part of its support during natural disasters.

Hurricane Melissa’s Impact

Hurricane Melissa struck Jamaica as a Category 5 hurricane in late October 2025. The storm caused widespread damage, prompting the mortgage relief.

In addition, the moratorium and waiver aim to ease financial stress. Still, the debt itself remains, but payments are deferred.

Announcement and Reporting

Prime Minister Andrew Holness announced the waiver on 6 June 2026. The Jamaica Gleaner and Caribbean News Global reported on it again on 21 and 22 August 2026.

Moreover, the state minister Fitz-Henley provided the beneficiary count in Parliament. This confirms the scale of the relief.

What This Means for Homeowners

For affected homeowners, the waiver means lower costs during recovery. Instead of paying peril insurance premiums, they can focus on rebuilding.

Even so, the waiver is limited to the moratorium period. After April 2026, regular payments resume.

How the Waiver Works

The National Housing Trust typically charges peril insurance premiums to borrowers. However, for the six-month period, these charges were waived.

In short, the trust absorbed the cost of J$585 million. This is a direct financial benefit to about 36,000 mortgages.

Overall Impact of the National Housing Trust

Overall, the National Housing Trust shows its commitment to disaster relief. By waiving premiums, it reduces the burden on storm-affected families.

Although the debt is not cancelled, the pause and waiver provide breathing room. Therefore, this measure supports recovery and stability.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the National Housing Trust?

The National Housing Trust is Jamaica’s state housing agency. It is funded by contributions from workers and employers and lends for home purchase and construction.

How much did the National Housing Trust waive?

The trust waived about J$585 million in peril-insurance costs. This applies to mortgage holders who benefited from the six-month moratorium after Hurricane Melissa.

Who is eligible for the waiver?

The waiver covers mortgage holders in affected areas who received the six-month moratorium. About 36,000 mortgages benefited from that pause, according to state minister Fitz-Henley.

Does the moratorium cancel the debt?

No, a moratorium is a pause on payments. It stops instalments falling due for a set period, but the debt remains.

Sources: Jamaica Gleaner; Caribbean News Global; Jamaica Observer.

World.content:

Key Facts — Spectrum award Viettel Global won a tender for three radio-frequency bands in the Dominican Republic, announced on 21 August 2026.

— Concession terms The 20-year concession covers 240 MHz across the 700 MHz, 2300 MHz, and C-Band 3.6 GHz bands.

— Regulator INDOTEL issued Resolution 073-2026 on 19 August 2026 under International Public Tender Indotel/LPI-001-2026.

— Services Viettel plans to offer 4G and 5G mobile and public telecom services using the awarded spectrum.

— Investment An industry report cites an approved investment plan of about US$560 million for the Dominican launch.

The Vietnamese group will need to invest about US$560 million to enter a market where Claro and Altice dominate.

Viettel has won spectrum in the Dominican Republic and will become the country’s fourth mobile operator. The award is a regulatory step, not a commercial launch, and no start date has been announced.

Viettel Wins Spectrum Tender

Viettel Global, a subsidiary of Vietnam’s Viettel Military Industry and Telecoms Group. Won a tender for the right to use three radio-frequency bands in the Dominican Republic.

The announcement came on 21 August 2026, according to official statements. This is a spectrum award and concession step, not a commercial launch of services.

Therefore, customers will have to wait for the network to go live.

Details of the Spectrum Concession

Viettel Global obtained rights to 240 MHz of spectrum, in the 700 MHz. 2300 MHz and C-Band 3.6 GHz bands, under a 20-year concession.

The regulator INDOTEL issued Resolution 073-2026 on 19 August 2026, as part of International Public Tender Indotel/LPI-001-2026. In addition, the planned services are 4G and 5G mobile and public telecom services using the awarded spectrum.

In short, this gives Viettel the foundation to build a modern network.

Viettel’s Expansion in the Americas

Viettel and news releases state the Dominican Republic will be Viettel’s eleventh international telecom market. And its third in the Americas, once operations start.

Its other markets in the Americas are Peru and Haiti. Meanwhile, this expansion reflects Viettel’s strategy to grow beyond its home base.

However, the company has not yet revealed a consumer-facing brand for the Dominican market.

Investment and Market Entry

An industry report cites an approved Viettel investment plan of about US$560 million for the Dominican launch. That is a serious commitment for a market that is already concentrated.

As a result, Viettel would become the country’s fourth mobile operator. By contrast, the market is highly concentrated, with Claro as leader, Altice a strong second, and a smaller third player.

Understanding Spectrum and Its Role

Spectrum is the range of radio frequencies a mobile network uses. Governments auction it because there is a finite amount, and without it an operator cannot run a network.

For example, the 700 MHz band offers good coverage, while the 3.6 GHz band supports high-speed 5G. So Viettel’s mix of bands should help it deliver both reach and capacity.

What This Means for Consumers

Dominicans may eventually have a new choice for mobile services, but no launch date has been set. Still, the investment signals a long-term commitment.

Moreover, a fourth operator could increase competition over time. Even so, the market leaders are well established, so Viettel will need to differentiate itself.

Regulatory Process and Next Steps

The award came through Resolution 073-2026, issued by INDOTEL on 19 August 2026, as part of International Public Tender Indotel/LPI-001-2026. This is a formal step in the licensing process.

After the concession, Viettel must still build its network and obtain any additional approvals. Therefore, the commercial launch will likely take time.

Viettel’s Global Footprint

Viettel already operates in Peru and Haiti, so it knows the region. This new market will be its eleventh international telecom market.

In fact, the company is one of Vietnam’s largest telecom groups. However, the full list of its markets has not been disclosed in official statements.

Looking Ahead for Viettel

The spectrum award is a milestone, but the hard work begins now. Viettel must deploy equipment, hire staff, and market its services.

Once operations start, it will become the fourth operator in a market that needs more competition. Overall, this is a big bet on the Dominican Republic’s future.

Frequently Asked Questions

What spectrum did Viettel win in the Dominican Republic?

Viettel Global won rights to 240 MHz of spectrum in the 700 MHz, 2300 MHz, and C-Band 3.6 GHz bands. The concession lasts 20 years.

When will Viettel launch services in the Dominican Republic?

No launch date has been announced. The spectrum award is a regulatory step, not a commercial launch.

How much will Viettel invest in the Dominican Republic?

An industry report cites an approved investment plan of about US$560 million for the Dominican launch. This is a significant commitment.

Will Viettel be the fourth mobile operator in the Dominican Republic?

Yes, Viettel would become the country’s fourth mobile operator once operations start. The market is currently led by Claro, with Altice as a strong second.

Sources: INDOTEL; Viettel releases; telecom trade press.

JPMorgan now expects Dominican Republic growth of around 4.5% in 2026, according to a bank statement. The figure is slightly above its own July projection of 4.3% and well above the central bank’s forecast.

JPMorgan Raises Dominican Republic Growth Forecast

JPMorgan’s latest estimate puts Dominican Republic growth at around 4.5% for 2026. This is a modest upgrade from the 4.3% it had projected in July.

The bank’s representatives shared the forecast during a working meeting with Banco de Reservas. Known as Banreservas, in Santo Domingo on 22 August 2026.

They also said JPMorgan wants to expand its investments in the country.

Strong First Half Drives the Upgrade

The bank links its interest to the country’s recent performance. Growth hit 6.4% year on year in June, and 4.5% in the first half of 2026.

Inflation is also easing, now running at about 4.2% year on year. These figures help explain why JPMorgan is more optimistic than other institutions.

How JPMorgan’s View Compares With Others

The International Monetary Fund projects 4.0% growth for 2026. The central bank, the BCRD, sees a range of 3.5% to 4.0%.

Therefore, JPMorgan’s estimate stands at the top of the range. It is also above the Latin American and Caribbean average, as Finance Minister Magín Díaz noted in July.

Deepening an Existing Presence

JPMorgan has a longstanding correspondent banking relationship with Banreservas, running for several years. This is a deepening of an existing presence rather than a new entry.

A correspondent bank handles cross-border payments and dollar clearing for a local bank. In short, it is plumbing rather than retail banking, but vital for moving money abroad.

Recent Deal Highlights Confidence

In August 2026, JPMorgan acted as joint lead arranger, bookrunner and structuring agent for a US$902.3 million financing. The deal supports the Manzanillo LNG-to-power project.

This role shows the bank’s commitment to the Dominican Republic’s energy sector. It also complements the positive growth outlook.

What the Meeting Signaled

The working meeting in Santo Domingo focused on expanding investments. However, no specific amounts or sectors were disclosed.

Still, the message was clear: JPMorgan sees opportunity in the country. The growth forecast and the LNG deal both point in that direction.

The Broader Economic Picture

With inflation easing and growth strong, the Dominican economy is performing well. The first half of 2026 already showed 4.5% expansion.

Meanwhile, the IMF’s 4.0% projection is more conservative. Yet even that is above the regional average, according to the finance minister.

What This Means for Investors

For foreign investors, a higher growth forecast can signal a stable environment. JPMorgan’s upgrade may attract more attention to the country.

In addition, the correspondent banking relationship ensures smooth dollar transactions. This reduces friction for businesses operating locally.

Outlook for the Rest of 2026

JPMorgan’s 4.5% forecast is slightly above its own earlier projection. The bank appears confident that momentum will hold.

As a result, the Dominican Republic growth story remains positive. The next months will show whether the country meets these expectations.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is JPMorgan’s latest growth forecast for the Dominican Republic?

JPMorgan expects Dominican Republic growth of around 4.5% in 2026. This is up from its July projection of 4.3%.

How does JPMorgan’s forecast compare with the IMF’s?

The IMF projects 4.0% growth for 2026, which is lower than JPMorgan’s 4.5%. The central bank’s forecast is even lower, at 3.5% to 4.0%.

Why is JPMorgan interested in the Dominican Republic?

The bank cites strong recent performance, including 6.4% growth in June and easing inflation. It also has a long-standing relationship with Banreservas.

What role did JPMorgan play in the Manzanillo project?

In August 2026, JPMorgan acted as joint lead arranger, bookrunner and structuring agent for a US$902.3 million financing. This supports the LNG-to-power project.
