World.title: Once sleepy and run-down, Italy’s largest island is full of wonders
World.content:
On this visit, I’m keen to see how much Sicily has changed, explore the island’s fascinating history and visit some of the famous archaeological sites, some of the richest in the Mediterranean.

Back then Sicily was sleepy, intriguing, a little run-down perhaps, with pompous architecture and a taste for elaborate funerals. And like many travellers my view of modern Sicily is, perhaps inevitably, largely shaped by the prism of The Godfather movies and blood-stained news coverage of the Mafia, which culminated in the tortuous Maxi Trails of the 1990s.

I’d visited Sicily many years ago and carry vivid memories of hanging out in Palermo before taking a very slow train (where is Mussolini when you need him?) to Naples, via a ferry across the Straits of Messina.

After a quick shower, I’m wandering the deserted streets of this honey-coloured southern Italian city. Camera in hand I snap almost everything I see from the boat-bobbing harbour to the flowering oleanders, the grand squares, picturesque alleyways and Baroque cathedral.

It’s just after 4am when I open my eyes to a strange, dimly lit hotel room. After a 29-hour trek from Australia my body clock is all over the place, but for once, I’m pleased to have a touch of jet lag. I throw the shutters of my room wide open to find Syracuse bathed in delicious golden light and strangely quiet – a deep, almost sinister, air of tranquillity that is distinctively Sicilian.

After a leisurely breakfast at the hotel, we board the minibus which will be our constant companion for the next week. There’s a short drive to the Parco Archeologico della Neapolis on the outskirts of Syracuse. It’s just after 9am, but the place is already packed. “Syracuse is a tourist town,” says Rosalia. “It’s always very busy here.”

“We Sicilians have been so many things over the centuries,” she explains. “We have been Greeks, Romans, Phoenicians – you name it. But I’m glad to say the Barbarians didn’t leave a lasting impression.”

After a 60-minute drive from Catania airport, I join my 14 travel companions, a friendly English bunch of various ages, for a glass of prosecco and a chat in the hotel dining room. I also meet our tour guide Rosalia Coci, a petite woman with huge knowledge of Sicilian history and a passion for archaeology. Her English is excellent and colourful.

The ancient Greek Temple of Concordia, near the city Agrigento, was built in the 5th century BC.

While my preference is to travel independently, the company’s Classic Sicily tour includes some of Sicily’s most important sites, including the Valley of the Temples and Villa Romana del Casale, while also showcasing the island’s mountain villages, stunning coastline and impeccable Norman and Baroque towns – impossible to do as a solo traveller.

I’m here to join an eight-day tour of the island run by Cox & Kings. Founded in 1758, the company built its reputation on these specialist, small group European itineraries, so I expect a busy schedule, decent hotels, reliable transport and expert commentary.

I’m particularly intrigued by the Triumphal Arch which dates from the Bourbon kingship. Noto is a pedestrian zone, and it’s pleasant to wander along Corso Vittorio Emanuele, visit a couple of churches, and then sit on a restaurant terrace with a cold Messina beer and soak up the atmosphere.

Then it’s time for our afternoon tour of Noto, a UNESCO-listed hilltop town south-west of Syracuse. The original Roman city was destroyed by an earthquake in 1693 and rebuilt in the Baroque style. The use of honey-coloured limestone gives Noto a sense of warmth, but its civic buildings are grand and opulent.

We return to Syracuse for lunch and are free to explore the old part of the city, Ortigia, which contains several important sites, including the Temple of Apollo and the impressive seventh century cathedral. Returning to the hotel, I stumble on a small beach packed with sunbathers, a reminder that the European summer is already here.

The Ear of Dionysius is an artificial limestone cave carved out of the Temenites Hill in Syracuse.

Despite its garden-like appearance, the archaeological park is brimming with all kinds of wonders, including a Greek theatre, a Roman amphitheatre and a vast quarry dating back to the fifth century BC. The quarry’s most famous attraction is the so-called Ear of Dionysius, an artificial cavity in the rock, but the horror of this place is palpable. “Around 7000 Carthaginian prisoners of war were sent here,” says Rosalia. “They were used as slave labour and worked to death.”

Sadly, I miss out on both the massive cathedral and Catania’s favourite snack of roasted peppers and tripe but do squeeze in a visit to the Roman Amphitheatre, one of the largest in Italy.

Today Catania is celebrated for its festivals, street food and fish market but will certainly wow lovers of architectural excess. I’m so smitten with the giant elephant sculpture in Piazza Duomo that I become separated from the rest of the party. After a few text messages we’re reunited, but I realise how dependent I’ve become on my fellow travellers.

Catania’s Piazza del Duomo is home to the city’s Elephant Statue and the Cathedral of Santa Agatha.

“The Greek history of the town is a series of invasions and destruction, but it became much more important during the Roman times under emperor Augustus,” explains Rosalia.

The distinctive shape of Mount Etna looms over Catania, Sicily’s second-largest city, and has played a major role in its history. When Catania was not being laid waste by invading armies, it was threatened by volcanic lava and earthquakes. A huge quake in 1693 flattened most of the city.

Rosalia warns us that today is going to involve a fair amount of travel as we venture north to Catania, a major provincial centre, and then onto Palermo, the capital of Sicily, with a lunch stop at Cefalu, a popular beach resort.

The day begins with a 30-minute drive up to Monreale, a beautifully preserved Norman town in the hills above Palermo. On the city outskirts we see some of the country estates that once belonged to Palermo’s richest families and one gifted to Lord Nelson, where he scandalised English society by carrying out a passionate affair with Lady Hamilton.

While the major streets are busier and scruffier than I remember, the cathedrals, palaces, squares and public gardens look newly scrubbed.

Cox & Kings step up the accommodation for our time in Palermo. Housed in a former bank, the Grand Hotel Piazza Borsa is certainly grand with a delightful central courtyard and rooms like small apartments. It’s also terribly formal – staff don formal attire to serve breakfast.

After driving through wheat fields and rolling farmland we reach Cefalu. With its umbrella packed beach and cobbled alleyways this sunny village is the ideal place to kick back. I find a small bistro and order a plate of sardines and a glass of chilled Sicilian white. Bellissimo.

It’s a 185-kilometre drive north to Cefalu which provides ample time to learn more about the Norman kings who unified Sicily and ruled over the island for 133 years.

Monreale is a beautifully preserved Norman town in the hills above the Sicilian capital of Palermo. iStock

The Cathedral of Santa Maria la Nuova in Monreale was a passion project for William The Good, King of Sicily, and blends Islamic and Norman architectural influences. This remarkable structure, which is beautifully preserved, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2015.

Returning to Palermo we visit the Norman cathedral, or duomo, and the sprawling Palazzo dei Normanni, which includes the Cappella Palatine.

The interior of the chapel is covered with elaborate Byzantine-style mosaics representing scenes from the Old Testament. “This chapel was commissioned by Roger II [in 1130] and is quite remarkable,” says Rosalia. “The mosaics depict all the church fathers. Here you see St John, St Gregory and St Basil.”

Palermo’s stunning 12th century Palatine Chapel is a mix of Byzantine, Norman, and Fatimid architectural styles . Shutterstock

We stop for a light lunch at a family-run restaurant before continuing our walking tour of Palermo. I persuade Rosalia to take a detour to the Monastery of Santa Caterina which is renowned for its cannoli – classic famous Sicilian pastries made of tube-shaped, deep-fried pastry dough shells filled with ricotta cheese – but we leave empty-handed. “There is no cannoli today,” she says. “Palermo has a water shortage and the bakery cannot operate.”

DAY FOUR | Of vanished cities and hilltop towns | Segesta + Erice

After another sumptuous breakfast at Grand Hotel Piazza Borsa, we board the minibus for a long drive that will take us across the top of Sicily and down the east coast to Segesta, stepping off point for the Valley of the Temples.

The terrain is harsher and drier here, but we are soon rewarded by our first glimpse of the Doric temple at Segesta, one of the best-preserved Athenian temples in the Mediterranean.

Near to the area’s Doric temple, the well-preserved Greek Theatre of Segesta occupies the summit of the 440-metre-high Monte Barbaro. iStock

The remote, rural location adds to the sense of drama as we walk up to the temple which was built between 430 and 420 BC. Although Greek in style, the original settlers are thought to have been Trojan exiles. “The temple looks impressive, but it was never actually finished,” says Rosalia. “There were so many wars and other issues going on.”

Segesta was once the centre of the enigmatic Elymian civilisation, said to have been founded by Trojan exiles who were constantly shifting their allegiance between Rome and Carthage.

Today’s visitor enjoys a sense of serenity that the original settlers clearly never experience. The city that once stood here has vanished, so running your hands along one of these ancient columns is a bitter-sweet sensation.

Next stop is Erice, a flawless Sicilian village perched atop Mount Erice and commanding stunning views over the city of Trapani. “I think you will like Erice,” says Rosalia. “Because everyone likes it.” Fans of Erice include the poet Virgil who mentions the town in his famous work, the Aeneid, but its history stretches back to the Elymian and Phoenician times. Later came the Arabs, Normans and Spanish.

An ancient medieval cobblestone backstreet in Erice, a charming village set at 750 metres above sea level. iStock

With its cobbled streets, alleyways, cafes and souvenir shops, Erice attracts plenty of tourists, but retains a relaxed, charming atmosphere. History buffs can explore the town’s two forts, one Saracen and the other Norman, or just sit on the old ramparts and enjoy the views.

DAY FIVE | On an amble through antiquity | Agrigento + Valley of the Temples

The Temple of Juno in the Valley of the Temples, close to the Sicilian hilltop city of Agrigento. Getty Images

The town of Agrigento serves as our base from which to explore the Valley of the Temples, the centrepiece of this Classic Sicily itinerary.

This arid valley, dotted with almond trees, features eight Greek Doric temples dating back to the sixth century BC. Lost for centuries, these temples were only rediscovered by archaeologists in the 18th century.

“After the Greek period, the Romans built a 12-kilometre wall around the park, but the temples later fell into disrepair – the Temple of Concordia was converted into a church and is the best preserved,” says Rosalia.

Our morning saunter through the Valley of Temples is the most arduous of the entire trip but is exhilarating and informative. Our legs and brains are both aching as we drive to a small trattoria in the countryside between Agrigento and Piazza Armerina. For lunch, we have plates of hearty beef ragu and slices of chilled melon for dessert.

Two hours later we’re deposited at yet another archaeological site, but one that almost eclipses the Valley of the Temples. Dating from the fourth century, Villa Romana del Casale was once the centre of a vast estate. Buried under tonnes of mud by a flood in the 12th century, the property was rediscovered 700 years later, its beautiful mosaics as vibrant as ever.

One of the treasured mosaics from Villa Romana del Casale, near Piazza Armerina. iStock

Gazing down at the depictions of everyday Roman life, sea voyages, exotic African animals and lady athletes (the so-called bikini girls) is truly spine-tingling, transporting the viewer to a world so removed from our own.

“We believe this was a summer residence for a wealthy man,” says Rosalia. “The property is divided into several parts. There are the owner’s private apartments, an area for guests, a gymnasium, a banqueting hall and thermal baths which were open to the public.”

DAY SIX | Under the volcano | Taormina + Mount Etna

After the sensory and intellectual riches of the past five days, I’d imagined that the pace would slow down. How wrong could I be? The previous evening we’d driven to the medieval town of Taormina. A Sicilian version of Capri, this hilltop honeypot just oozes style, sophistication and money. An episode of The White Lotus was filmed at the Four Seasons Hotel here and at the town’s magnificent Teatro Greco.

Taormina, Mount Etna and the Ionian Sea from Piazza IX Aprile. iStock

Over the centuries Taormina has attracted European royalty, artists, movie stars and writers. D.H. Lawrence and his wife Frieda lived here for two years and I managed to track down his old house – now locked up – which has fine views over the Ionian Sea. “We love Taormina and in particular our house,” he wrote. “I love [watching] the sun rise over the open sea to the east.”

Visitors stroll through the pedestrianised main street of Taormina near to its city gate. iStock

Our lodging is called Hotel Splendid and shares the same jaw-dropping vista that Lawrence enjoyed. After breakfast, we’re off for a morning tour of Mount Etna, Europe’s highest (3327 metres) active volcano – its last eruptions were in 2001 and 2002.

The drive takes us up through vineyards, citrus orchards and neat little villages. The rich volcanic soil is responsible for the area’s abundance of cherries, hazelnuts, pears, strawberries, pistachios and, of course, grapes.

“A national park was established in 1987 which covers Mount Etna and also protects all the communities that exist on its slopes,” says Rosalia.

After pulling into the visitor centre, we spend a happy hour clambering around its bare, greyish slopes and photographing the moon-like craters. Our lunchtime stop is at Murgo Wines, one of 150 vineyards in the Mount Etna DOC, where we enjoy platters of cured meats, cheese and pickled vegetables and get to sample some estate wines, including a refreshing Etna rosso and an inky cabernet sauvignon from its Catania vineyards.

Gazing down over the plains below us this seems like the perfect place to say farewell to Sicily, but we have a full afternoon of sightseeing in Taormina before us. After seven days on the road, we’re still eager to see more.

Five more things to see and do in Sicily

Escape to the Aeolian Islands

Older Sicilians go all misty eyed at the mention of the Aeolian Islands. Known locally as the Seven Sisters, the archipelago off the north-eastern tip of Sicily has been a favourite holiday haunt for decades. Volcano Island, the closest to Sicily, offers the rare chance to hike on an active volcano plus taking a soak in the island’s health-giving thermal springs.

Sicily’s most charming village

Sick of fighting the crowds in Taormina? Then head up the hill to the medieval village of Castelmola. Built around a ruined Norman castle, the village is remarkably unspoilt, with picturesque terrace houses, narrow alleyways and several ancient churches. Visitors who hike the five kilometres from Taormina are rewarded with sweeping views of Mount Etna and the Straits of Messina.

Enna: A city in the sky

At 931 metres, Enna is Italy’s highest provincial city and one packed with ancient monuments and archaeological sites. Known as “the navel of Sicily” Enna is a stunning mountain town but attracts few tourists because of its remote location. Over the centuries, Enna has been ruled by the Greeks, the Romans, the Byzantines, the Arabs and the Normans who have all left their mark. Its many attractions include Italy’s largest medieval castle (Castello di Lombardia), a 14th century cathedral, and a temple site dedicated to Demeter. It also stages several dramatic religious festivals, including Madonna of the Visitation.

Hike Cavagrande del Cassibile

Cavagrande del Cassibile is a nature reserve near the towns of Avola, Noto, and Syracuse. Keen walkers can join a guided hike along a 10-kilometre stretch of the Cassibile River. The path passes through canyons and scrub and ends at the Cavagrande lakes. Other attractions include the necropolis of Cassibile, an archaeological site boasting a large system of caves and tunnels.

The world’s most beautiful city

Destroyed by a 1693 earthquake, Scicli was rebuilt in Baroque style. The writer Elio Vittorini described the resultant civic masterwork, 25 kilometres south of Ragusa, as perhaps “the most beautiful city in the world”. Today’s visitors to the town enjoy a wealth of ecclesiastic architecture, fine boulevards and imposing town squares set in a dramatic gorge.

THE DETAILS

TOUR

Classic Sicily is an eight-day Cox & Kings tour of the Mediterranean’s largest island visiting the key historical and archaeological sites, from Syracuse in the east to Erice in the west. Prices start from $5995 a person and include four-star accommodation, all entrance fees, breakfasts and some meals, private transport and a tour guide. See coxandkingtravel.com

FLY

Cathay Pacific flies from Sydney and Melbourne to Rome via Hong Kong several times each week, with connecting ITA Airways flights to Catania-Fontanarossa Airport. See cathaypacific.com

MORE

visitsicily.info/en

The writer travelled as a guest of Cox & Kings Australia.

World.title: The other Australian Wolverine: Liam McIntyre on donning the adamantium claws
World.content:
TechnologyVideo games The other Australian Wolverine: Liam McIntyre on donning the adamantium claws Tim Biggs August 23, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than 25 years after Hugh Jackman first portrayed the character, another Australian actor is stepping into the yellow armour of one of Marvel’s most violent and most popular heroes. Liam McIntyre, 44, stars in Sony’s upcoming video game Marvel’s Wolverine, developed by Insomniac Games, creators of three highly acclaimed Spider-Man games. This new take on the character is bloody and action-packed, but has a complex emotional narrative at its core. A new PlayStation video game follows Wolverine as mutants and humanity clash for the first time. Set in a world where the X-Men don’t exist, and few people are even aware there are super-powered mutants among them, the game puts Logan — a practically indestructible mutant with retractable claws, traumatised by flashes of a past he can’t remember — in a power struggle between human and mutant factions who each want to eradicate the other’s species.



While there’s plenty of screaming and growling from McIntyre, his portrayal is more grounded and open than most. Still, as the character remains canonically Canadian, it begs the question; why do we keep seeing Australians in the role? “Australians don’t have a lot of self-importance. Tall poppy syndrome, help your mates out, that sort of thing,” said Mcintyre, in Melbourne to promote the game. “Wolverine is an unassuming, get-things-done kind of gruff, rugged [character]. I think his ethos aligns with what a lot of Australians view as some of the best qualities about ourselves. Maybe through that worldview, Australians are like, ‘I kind of think I get this guy’.” Liam McIntyre plays the unstoppable mutant in Marvel’s Wolverine. Despite Wolverine being a mutant, many stories feature him as a relatable, sympathetic character constantly under pressure. His abilities give him a responsibility to help people, but his powers also make him a liability. His lethality and animal-like instincts frequently open him up to manipulation from villains, and he’s only too aware of the possibility he could hurt the people he cares about.



In the game, Logan leaps around the screen tearing enemies apart, with consecutive kills filling a rage meter that unlocks even quicker and more violent attacks, and lets him shrug off damage. But we also see the character in quieter situations, struggling to understand his purpose. “A lot of superheroes have special powers, they’re doing special things and saving people, whereas it’s almost a burden for Logan. He’s most useful when he’s a weapon, that’s when he can enact the most change. But the way that he enacts that change takes a heavy toll on him,” McIntyre said. “He’s not necessarily excited to go out and save the world. He doesn’t want fanfare. He doesn’t want to get his name up in lights as a hero.” The camera is a lot closer, and the action a lot bloodier, than in Insomniac’s previous Spider-man games. McIntyre, born in Adelaide, has been based in the US since he was cast in the lead role of the Spartacus TV series in 2012. Since then, he’s had brushes with super-heroism in The Flash TV show and an animated Justice League feature, and he’s had success in video games as JD Fenix in the Gears of War series. But his latest role feels particularly special because he’s a long-time fan of Wolverine, and he’s still adjusting to seeing his face on the character.



At a preview event for the game at Marvel Stadium, the signboards and screens around the ground were all lit up with promotional images of the character. Sony has introduced special edition PlayStation 5 consoles with Wolverine printed on them. And at Disney’s recent D23 event in California, Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige introduced a look at the game on stage. “He pointed straight at my face! He might not have known that, but I mean, even tangentially, that’s just the wildest,” McIntyre said. “I was watching X-Men: The Animated Series as a 13-year-old thinking, ‘That Wolverine dude is cool.’ And now I’m here. There are these moments in your life where you’re just like, I can’t believe that guy became this guy. Me. It seems impossible.” Editor's pick Video games May the choice be with you: The next great Star Wars story might be a game Acting for blockbuster video games is no longer necessarily just about providing your voice and face. In addition to sound booth work, McIntyre spent four years off-and-on recording performance capture — which minutely tracks facial as well as whole-body movements — alongside stunt people and a core group of co-stars portraying mutants Sabretooth, Mystique and Jean Grey, who he says have all become friends.



But it was performing opposite prolific video game actor Troy Baker, who McIntyre has known for a long time, that he cites as a highlight of the process. “To work with someone who is that good is such a joy. He’s so in the moment, so fresh ... You don’t get many jobs like this in a career, where you really feel like everybody’s trying to make something truly special.” Releasing on September 15, the game comes at a time when Marvel’s also beginning to pull the X-Men and mutants into its big screen efforts. A key character featured in the game was also just introduced to the Marvel Cinematic Universe in Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Troy Baker’s character in the game is Nathaniel Essex, who in the comics becomes the villain Mister Sinister, who was just announced at D23 as heading to the MCU portrayed by Adam Driver. While Insomniac could not have known any of this during development, the game’s senior project director Jess Reiner-Reed said that these characters have decades of history, and that fans are happy to see multiple versions of them at once as long as the stories are compelling and ring true. “Having exposure around all these different characters only enriches the universe. We can take inspiration from the movies and TV shows, and they take some inspiration from us,” she said, referring to the well-documented impact of the Spider-Man video games on Brand New Day’s choreography and effects.



“Audiences trust the care we put into these uniquely Insomniac stories, and they can trust that we’re going to do the same thing with Wolverine.” Get news and reviews on technology, gadgets and gaming in our Technology newsletter every Friday. Sign up here.

World.title: High rents a roadblock to productivity
World.content:
NationalNSWRenting Editorial High rents a roadblock to productivity The Herald's View Editorial August 23, 2026 — 6:00am

August 23, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The interests of renters are often treated as a footnote in Sydney’s never-ending conversation about property prices. But even with the recent dip in house prices, buying a property remains out of reach for many – especially buying a home that is within reasonable reach of the workplace. Rents are high in central Sydney. Dominic Lorrimer New data revealed in The Sun-Herald today shows there has been little respite from rental rises across Sydney, with the price of owning your own home keeping large numbers of people in the rental market, especially in the inner cities where they compete with international students to lease apartments. Senior economics correspondent Shane Wright reports that in some parts of the country, rents have risen by 80 per cent since the COVID-era rent freeze.



In Zetland, Chippendale and Haymarket in inner Sydney, rents have jumped by between $367 and $452 a week, Wright reports. The picture is mixed, though, with some Sydney suburbs – such as Hunters Hill, Avalon Beach and Hornsby Heights – recording rental price growth slower than the city’s 23.6 per cent inflation rate since mid-2021. The NSW South Coast has bucked the national trend, with landlords in some towns asking less on average than they were in 2021. These falls are attributed to less demand since the COVID-era surge of people seeking to leave Sydney and Canberra. Effects of the current house price slump on the rental market are unclear, but in theory the slump may enable more renters to become home owners, which in turn would ease price pressure in the broader rental market.



There are many other factors at play, though, including federal changes to negative gearing that some fear will force landlords to lift rents to compensate for their lost tax breaks. Related Article Renting Rents spike up to 80 per cent as people are pushed from houses to units The national data that Wright reports on today suggests local factors – including proximity to major employment and education zones, transport and the regional cost of living – heavily influence how much landlords can charge. The most obvious remedy is to increase housing supply in areas where people want to live. In Sydney, the Minns government has taken steps in the right direction with its overhaul of the planning system and focus on transport-oriented development.



Higher densities are a central mechanism for solving the housing crisis for renters and home owners alike. Related Article Analysis

Home loans Five charts that explain what’s really happening with housing It is true that existing high-density areas of Sydney have been home to some of the nation’s biggest rent rises since COVID. But as more high-rise development takes place in well-located areas of the city, tenants will have more options and landlords can be expected to curb rent rises to attract them. Landlords need a fair return on their investment. But affordable housing lifts overall living standards and can benefit the wider economy, as people are able to spend more of their money on things other than housing.



Young people especially can be caught in the trap of paying high rents and being unable to save a deposit to get their feet on the first rungs of the property ladder. Everyone deserves a place to call home, and the end goal for policymakers must balance the needs of investors with equitable outcomes for ordinary residents of NSW. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Heather and Hugo met at drama school 40 years ago. They haven’t stopped working together since
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There is a familiarity within the Australian creative scene that gives audiences a unique kinship with the actors who appear on our screens and stages. These are the faces we have grown up with, who we have aged with, and who we innately feel like — were we to run into them at the pub — we could share a beer with. It gives our home-grown productions a warm, fuzzy feeling because, not only do we recognise familiar streets, landmarks and cafes used as filming locations, but we feel an instant intimacy when recognisable faces appear. The pride is palpable. Occasionally, a production comes along that is so successful in creating that feeling of familiarity you can’t help but smile when you watch it, even if the subject makes you cry or shift uncomfortably in your seat. And that, in a nutshell, is Dalliance. Hugo Weaving and Heather Mitchell in Dalliance. The good friends have worked together for more than 40 years. The six-episode drama series charts the fallout from one big, life-changing event and the ways it radically upends a group of 60-something friends. Exploring everything from female friendship and the path to parenthood to sex, desire and ambition, it’s the latest endeavour from John and Dan Edwards, the father-and-son production duo behind Bump and The F Ward. The series also marks a reunion for long-time friends and collaborators Heather Mitchell and Hugo Weaving, who star as would-be romantic interests, Dani and Billy. Their on-screen rapport is instant, but when you’ve shared stage and screen for over 40 years, that’s to be expected. Related Article Review What to stream this week: A juicy holiday-from-hell Brit drama, plus five more picks “I feel so blessed every time I get to work with him,” Mitchell says of her decades-long friend. “From when we first worked together … there’s always been a lot of laughter, a lot of fun and ease. It hasn’t changed, really, over the years. And that’s the thing about getting older. [With] people you’ve known for a long time, you sort of slot right back to where you were.”



The pair first met at the prestigious National Institute of Dramatic Art (NIDA) in 1979, began working together at Sydney Theatre Company in 1982, and, most recently, shared the screen in Binge’s acclaimed multi-generational drama Love Me. “I adore Heather,” says Weaving. “Working with her is being embraced. She has a capacity to care about others like no one else and I consider myself hugely lucky to get to play with her whenever we work together.” Georgie Parker as Rose, Hugo Weaving as Billy, and Heather Mitchell as Dani in Dalliance. Dalliance is a reunion for many of the cast, and remarkable in that most of them are in their 50s and 60s. Mitchell was most excited by the prospect of giving talented friends, such as Catherine McClements, an opportunity to expand their creative horizons. “I loved watching her play a character who’s sexy, funny and complex when she’s so often cast as brittle and tough.” She also knew the perfect person for the role of Rose, Billy’s wife of 40 years, pleading with Home and Away producer Julie McGauran to release Georgie Parker, who has spent 16 years working on the soap, for Dalliance. “I’ve known Georgie Parker since we were in our 20s, and I think this role shows people the depth of her talent.” Related Article Australian TV This TV legend has guided us through every decade of life. Next up? Our 60s By nature of the series’ time-jumping format, Weaving worked mostly with Mitchell and David Wenham, who plays Billy’s volatile younger brother, but relished the chance to connect with old friends. “Our read-through days were very special, all the cast together for two days. It was so lovely to catch up with everyone.” And like all great 21st-century friendships, Mitchell adds, the WhatsApp group is still going strong. “We’re constantly writing to each other on because we formed such a close relationship between all of us. It’s beautiful.”



For 68-year-old Mitchell, this was a project particularly close to her heart. Despite a career rich with experience (she won her second AACTA Award in February for The Narrow Road to the Deep North), this is her first time in the producer’s seat. She was quick to accept when John Edwards made the offer. “One of the beautiful things about being older is the challenges are less risky because you’ve got less to lose, if that makes sense.” “And I have loved it,” she adds, pointing out that her age gave her the confidence to ask questions. “I haven’t beaten myself up if I don’t know something. I just say, ‘Can you help me with this?’ I’d go to the production manager and say, ‘I have no idea what this means.’ I think as I’m getting older, I ask for help more.” Georgie Parker as Rose and David Wenham as Gary in Dalliance. Camaraderie played a pivotal role in not only the chemistry between the actors and behind the scenes – Mitchell’s husband of 34 years, Martin McGrath, is the show’s director of photography – but also in the writing room, where lived experience and a willingness to be vulnerable gave depth to each character’s journey. Related Article Opinion

Australian TV If you are still complaining about Australian TV, it’s time to shut up Louise Rugendyke National TV editor “We talked a lot about sexuality,” says Mitchell. “Passion, love, sex. People who’ve been through cancer, how medication affects your sexuality, how desire changes for each person as they get older. Some people just do not want to be touched any more. Other people long for it desperately. For me personally, I’m probably saying too much … [but] I’m more sexually satisfied in my 60s than I ever have been. And I know what I want. “We really wanted to explore both men and women and whatever gender, that there is no time limit to love and companionship and sex. And that sex is not the driving thing for everybody. That often people go online looking for very different things. And sometimes it is sex with no other attachments. And other times, someone is really looking for a true love. The past can turn up.



“So we talked at length about what is sexuality, and how is it perceived? And I would hope that for younger people, if any younger people watch this show, that they will also feel that life doesn’t stop. You don’t stop growing. You don’t stop living. You don’t stop wanting.” Mitchell and Weaving in the 1984 miniseries Bodyline. It was the first time they played partners on screen. Dalliance, and Mitchell’s own sharpened focus on life, touches on what psychologists call “socioemotional selectivity theory”. It argues that we shift our priorities and goals depending on how long we think we have left. Young people who see the future as long and open-ended prioritise knowledge and building their social network, while those further along in life, faced with their own mortality, grow more selective. They chase emotionally meaningful goals, avoid obvious risk, and prioritise close relationships over new connections. “The older you get, you’re looking closer to the idea of death. More friends die around you, more things happen which you might feel will result in an ending,” reflects Mitchell. “Certainly within this show, we want to say, no one’s ready to end anything. These characters aren’t thinking of endings, they’re thinking of beginnings, like how do I want to live the rest of my life? How do I want to be with the people I love?” Loading Endings, as it happens, are fresh in Mitchell’s mind. She recently starred in black comedy The Fox, which would become one of the late Sam Neill’s final roles (though with Neill as the voice of a magpie, they didn’t actually share the screen). “Sam was a very, very dear friend of mine,” says Mitchell, who also paid tribute to Neill at the recent Logie Awards. “I’ve spent a lot of time with him, and my husband was a close friend of Sam’s. He’s directed me, I’ve acted with him, but our main relationship is a non-professional one – I actually went out with him when I was 22 – and I still feel his presence enormously. “And there again, a man in his late 70s who was working and had jobs lined up. So much of his identity and his love was in his work, the people and the industry. I think it’s important for people to know, he was not a weakened person. He was strong right up until the end.”

World.title: The medal that will put Sydney on the map. The wrong map
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life The medal that will put Sydney on the map. The wrong map Julie Power August 23, 2026 — 9:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Sydney Marathon scheduled for next Sunday has again put the city on the map, but maybe not the right map. When organisers of the TCS Sydney Marathon unveiled the official 2026 medal that is engraved with the major landmarks along the 42.2 km course past the Sydney Opera House, the Harbour Bridge and St Mary’s Cathedral, marathon runners spotted a detour that could add substantial distance … and time. Sydney Marathon competitors will get this medal, complete with various icons of the city’s landmarks … plus a surprise. Instagram Instead of including Sydney’s Allianz Stadium on Moore Park Road, Centennial Park, they included the Allianz Arena in Munich, Germany, some 16, 404 km away. To be fair, they do share some similarities: Both are round, large and designed to disguise their size. Munich’s stadium is made from inflated plastic panels, while Sydney’s Allianz Stadium was designed to resemble a cloud.



News of the error has made headlines around the world. The BBC reported that one week out from the world-renowned Sydney Marathon, organisers faced questions about whether designers etched the wrong city’s stadium on the participation medal. On Morning Coffee Run, a popular social media account, the error attracted hundreds of comments and likes. Host James Dunn said it was a major mess up. “Oh dear this is bad … Because someone Google-searched the wrong thing and got the Allianz Arena rather than the Allianz Stadium, which is in Sydney,” he said. The German Allianz Arena responded with humour. “Oh wow, we didn’t have that on our bingo card! 😂 Perhaps they tried to find something else they had in common: Allianz Arena_____Sydney Opera House. Unique Architecture ______ Both are worth a visit!” The error was uncovered after organisers unveiled its official 2026 medal, urging the public to look closely to “find the story of the course in the details”.



It is the second major blooper to embarrass organisers of a marathon. Runners at the 2012 Edinburgh Marathon were embarrassed when presented with what appeared to be a penis-shaped medal. Organisers of the Sydney Marathon said the markings around the edge represent each kilometre of the course, while the eight circles on the back represent the World Marathon Majors. “A beautiful Sydney skyline brings the course to life, featuring the landmarks runners will experience along the way — starting with the Sydney Harbour Bridge and finishing at the world-famous Sydney Opera House,” the Marathon’s official account said. Joggers running across the Sydney Harbour Bridge in the 2025 Sydney Marathon. Getty



Starting in North Sydney and then crossing the Sydney Harbour Bridge, an estimated 100,000 - 150,000 people are expected to watch the race. This masthead sought a response from the Marathon’s organisers. An automatic reply said: “This year, we are expecting a record 40,000 participants on the start line, alongside unprecedented interest from media, partners and stakeholders. Race week will also see new entertainment precincts, live sites and performances across the city, as well as initiatives supporting local businesses.”

World.title: Father leaves seven-year-old son alone on Mount Fuji for hours
World.content:
WorldAsiaChild safety Father leaves seven-year-old son alone on Mount Fuji for hours Lily Shanagher August 23, 2026 — 8:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A man who left his seven-year-old son on Japan’s Mount Fuji alone for hours while he hiked has been reprimanded by police. The boy was taken into police custody after he was found sitting on a bench 2000 metres up Japan’s highest mountain in fog and rain with only a soft drink and a snack on Thursday morning. The boy, from Nagoya, said he had started climbing the hill with his 48-year-old father and his brother, but had complained of being too tired to continue. The boy was found on a bench 2000 metres up Japan’s highest mountain in fog and rain. Getty Images His father had told him to “wait here”, SBS TV reported, while he continued the 3700-metre ascent with his elder son, who had gone on ahead.



TV Asahi said the boy had been told to wait for hours at the sixth station of the mountain, with no money. Staff at a mountain hut alerted police to his presence after spotting him on his own at 7.30am local time (8.30am AEST). Officers contacted the father, who had reached the eighth station, and handed the boy over to him when he arrived back. Getty Images They invited the boy inside the hut and let him take shelter there while they waited for officers to arrive. Officers contacted the father, who had reached the eighth station, and handed the boy over to him when he arrived back.



It was estimated the boy had been left for about three hours, Japan Today reported. Editor's pick Foreign relations Taste testing the Japanese melon at the heart of a political stink The police officer told AFP that officers gave the man a scolding for leaving the child behind. “Even if it means having to give up on climbing the mountain together, leaving a child behind is unacceptable,” one told him, according to Japan Today. ‘Rash decision’



The father reportedly apologised to the police, admitting the act was careless. “I made a rash decision, and I deeply regret it,” he said. Editor's pick China It’s raining stars on big red mountain The family had reportedly been following the Fujinomiya route up the mountain beginning at the fifth station, which is accessible via public transport. It takes five hours to reach the peak from there and a further three hours to get down. Every year, about 200,000 people climb the mountain, which is a popular landmark in Japan and located on the island of Honshu, south-west of Tokyo.



It is one of three traditional “Holy Mountains” along with Mount Tate and Mount Haku in Toyama Prefecture and Honshu, respectively. It is an active volcano and was granted World Heritage Status in 2013. The Telegraph, London Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Once sleepy and run-down, Italy’s largest island is full of wonders
World.content:
On this visit, I’m keen to see how much Sicily has changed, explore the island’s fascinating history and visit some of the famous archaeological sites, some of the richest in the Mediterranean.

Back then Sicily was sleepy, intriguing, a little run-down perhaps, with pompous architecture and a taste for elaborate funerals. And like many travellers my view of modern Sicily is, perhaps inevitably, largely shaped by the prism of The Godfather movies and blood-stained news coverage of the Mafia, which culminated in the tortuous Maxi Trails of the 1990s.

I’d visited Sicily many years ago and carry vivid memories of hanging out in Palermo before taking a very slow train (where is Mussolini when you need him?) to Naples, via a ferry across the Straits of Messina.

After a quick shower, I’m wandering the deserted streets of this honey-coloured southern Italian city. Camera in hand I snap almost everything I see from the boat-bobbing harbour to the flowering oleanders, the grand squares, picturesque alleyways and Baroque cathedral.

It’s just after 4am when I open my eyes to a strange, dimly lit hotel room. After a 29-hour trek from Australia my body clock is all over the place, but for once, I’m pleased to have a touch of jet lag. I throw the shutters of my room wide open to find Syracuse bathed in delicious golden light and strangely quiet – a deep, almost sinister, air of tranquillity that is distinctively Sicilian.

After a leisurely breakfast at the hotel, we board the minibus which will be our constant companion for the next week. There’s a short drive to the Parco Archeologico della Neapolis on the outskirts of Syracuse. It’s just after 9am, but the place is already packed. “Syracuse is a tourist town,” says Rosalia. “It’s always very busy here.”

“We Sicilians have been so many things over the centuries,” she explains. “We have been Greeks, Romans, Phoenicians – you name it. But I’m glad to say the Barbarians didn’t leave a lasting impression.”

After a 60-minute drive from Catania airport, I join my 14 travel companions, a friendly English bunch of various ages, for a glass of prosecco and a chat in the hotel dining room. I also meet our tour guide Rosalia Coci, a petite woman with huge knowledge of Sicilian history and a passion for archaeology. Her English is excellent and colourful.

The ancient Greek Temple of Concordia, near the city Agrigento, was built in the 5th century BC.

While my preference is to travel independently, the company’s Classic Sicily tour includes some of Sicily’s most important sites, including the Valley of the Temples and Villa Romana del Casale, while also showcasing the island’s mountain villages, stunning coastline and impeccable Norman and Baroque towns – impossible to do as a solo traveller.

I’m here to join an eight-day tour of the island run by Cox & Kings. Founded in 1758, the company built its reputation on these specialist, small group European itineraries, so I expect a busy schedule, decent hotels, reliable transport and expert commentary.

I’m particularly intrigued by the Triumphal Arch which dates from the Bourbon kingship. Noto is a pedestrian zone, and it’s pleasant to wander along Corso Vittorio Emanuele, visit a couple of churches, and then sit on a restaurant terrace with a cold Messina beer and soak up the atmosphere.

Then it’s time for our afternoon tour of Noto, a UNESCO-listed hilltop town south-west of Syracuse. The original Roman city was destroyed by an earthquake in 1693 and rebuilt in the Baroque style. The use of honey-coloured limestone gives Noto a sense of warmth, but its civic buildings are grand and opulent.

We return to Syracuse for lunch and are free to explore the old part of the city, Ortigia, which contains several important sites, including the Temple of Apollo and the impressive seventh century cathedral. Returning to the hotel, I stumble on a small beach packed with sunbathers, a reminder that the European summer is already here.

The Ear of Dionysius is an artificial limestone cave carved out of the Temenites Hill in Syracuse.

Despite its garden-like appearance, the archaeological park is brimming with all kinds of wonders, including a Greek theatre, a Roman amphitheatre and a vast quarry dating back to the fifth century BC. The quarry’s most famous attraction is the so-called Ear of Dionysius, an artificial cavity in the rock, but the horror of this place is palpable. “Around 7000 Carthaginian prisoners of war were sent here,” says Rosalia. “They were used as slave labour and worked to death.”

Sadly, I miss out on both the massive cathedral and Catania’s favourite snack of roasted peppers and tripe but do squeeze in a visit to the Roman Amphitheatre, one of the largest in Italy.

Today Catania is celebrated for its festivals, street food and fish market but will certainly wow lovers of architectural excess. I’m so smitten with the giant elephant sculpture in Piazza Duomo that I become separated from the rest of the party. After a few text messages we’re reunited, but I realise how dependent I’ve become on my fellow travellers.

Catania’s Piazza del Duomo is home to the city’s Elephant Statue and the Cathedral of Santa Agatha.

“The Greek history of the town is a series of invasions and destruction, but it became much more important during the Roman times under emperor Augustus,” explains Rosalia.

The distinctive shape of Mount Etna looms over Catania, Sicily’s second-largest city, and has played a major role in its history. When Catania was not being laid waste by invading armies, it was threatened by volcanic lava and earthquakes. A huge quake in 1693 flattened most of the city.

Rosalia warns us that today is going to involve a fair amount of travel as we venture north to Catania, a major provincial centre, and then onto Palermo, the capital of Sicily, with a lunch stop at Cefalu, a popular beach resort.

The day begins with a 30-minute drive up to Monreale, a beautifully preserved Norman town in the hills above Palermo. On the city outskirts we see some of the country estates that once belonged to Palermo’s richest families and one gifted to Lord Nelson, where he scandalised English society by carrying out a passionate affair with Lady Hamilton.

While the major streets are busier and scruffier than I remember, the cathedrals, palaces, squares and public gardens look newly scrubbed.

Cox & Kings step up the accommodation for our time in Palermo. Housed in a former bank, the Grand Hotel Piazza Borsa is certainly grand with a delightful central courtyard and rooms like small apartments. It’s also terribly formal – staff don formal attire to serve breakfast.

After driving through wheat fields and rolling farmland we reach Cefalu. With its umbrella packed beach and cobbled alleyways this sunny village is the ideal place to kick back. I find a small bistro and order a plate of sardines and a glass of chilled Sicilian white. Bellissimo.

It’s a 185-kilometre drive north to Cefalu which provides ample time to learn more about the Norman kings who unified Sicily and ruled over the island for 133 years.

Monreale is a beautifully preserved Norman town in the hills above the Sicilian capital of Palermo. iStock

The Cathedral of Santa Maria la Nuova in Monreale was a passion project for William The Good, King of Sicily, and blends Islamic and Norman architectural influences. This remarkable structure, which is beautifully preserved, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2015.

Returning to Palermo we visit the Norman cathedral, or duomo, and the sprawling Palazzo dei Normanni, which includes the Cappella Palatine.

The interior of the chapel is covered with elaborate Byzantine-style mosaics representing scenes from the Old Testament. “This chapel was commissioned by Roger II [in 1130] and is quite remarkable,” says Rosalia. “The mosaics depict all the church fathers. Here you see St John, St Gregory and St Basil.”

Palermo’s stunning 12th century Palatine Chapel is a mix of Byzantine, Norman, and Fatimid architectural styles . Shutterstock

We stop for a light lunch at a family-run restaurant before continuing our walking tour of Palermo. I persuade Rosalia to take a detour to the Monastery of Santa Caterina which is renowned for its cannoli – classic famous Sicilian pastries made of tube-shaped, deep-fried pastry dough shells filled with ricotta cheese – but we leave empty-handed. “There is no cannoli today,” she says. “Palermo has a water shortage and the bakery cannot operate.”

DAY FOUR | Of vanished cities and hilltop towns | Segesta + Erice

After another sumptuous breakfast at Grand Hotel Piazza Borsa, we board the minibus for a long drive that will take us across the top of Sicily and down the east coast to Segesta, stepping off point for the Valley of the Temples.

The terrain is harsher and drier here, but we are soon rewarded by our first glimpse of the Doric temple at Segesta, one of the best-preserved Athenian temples in the Mediterranean.

Near to the area’s Doric temple, the well-preserved Greek Theatre of Segesta occupies the summit of the 440-metre-high Monte Barbaro. iStock

The remote, rural location adds to the sense of drama as we walk up to the temple which was built between 430 and 420 BC. Although Greek in style, the original settlers are thought to have been Trojan exiles. “The temple looks impressive, but it was never actually finished,” says Rosalia. “There were so many wars and other issues going on.”

Segesta was once the centre of the enigmatic Elymian civilisation, said to have been founded by Trojan exiles who were constantly shifting their allegiance between Rome and Carthage.

Today’s visitor enjoys a sense of serenity that the original settlers clearly never experience. The city that once stood here has vanished, so running your hands along one of these ancient columns is a bitter-sweet sensation.

Next stop is Erice, a flawless Sicilian village perched atop Mount Erice and commanding stunning views over the city of Trapani. “I think you will like Erice,” says Rosalia. “Because everyone likes it.” Fans of Erice include the poet Virgil who mentions the town in his famous work, the Aeneid, but its history stretches back to the Elymian and Phoenician times. Later came the Arabs, Normans and Spanish.

An ancient medieval cobblestone backstreet in Erice, a charming village set at 750 metres above sea level. iStock

With its cobbled streets, alleyways, cafes and souvenir shops, Erice attracts plenty of tourists, but retains a relaxed, charming atmosphere. History buffs can explore the town’s two forts, one Saracen and the other Norman, or just sit on the old ramparts and enjoy the views.

DAY FIVE | On an amble through antiquity | Agrigento + Valley of the Temples

The Temple of Juno in the Valley of the Temples, close to the Sicilian hilltop city of Agrigento. Getty Images

The town of Agrigento serves as our base from which to explore the Valley of the Temples, the centrepiece of this Classic Sicily itinerary.

This arid valley, dotted with almond trees, features eight Greek Doric temples dating back to the sixth century BC. Lost for centuries, these temples were only rediscovered by archaeologists in the 18th century.

“After the Greek period, the Romans built a 12-kilometre wall around the park, but the temples later fell into disrepair – the Temple of Concordia was converted into a church and is the best preserved,” says Rosalia.

Our morning saunter through the Valley of Temples is the most arduous of the entire trip but is exhilarating and informative. Our legs and brains are both aching as we drive to a small trattoria in the countryside between Agrigento and Piazza Armerina. For lunch, we have plates of hearty beef ragu and slices of chilled melon for dessert.

Two hours later we’re deposited at yet another archaeological site, but one that almost eclipses the Valley of the Temples. Dating from the fourth century, Villa Romana del Casale was once the centre of a vast estate. Buried under tonnes of mud by a flood in the 12th century, the property was rediscovered 700 years later, its beautiful mosaics as vibrant as ever.

One of the treasured mosaics from Villa Romana del Casale, near Piazza Armerina. iStock

Gazing down at the depictions of everyday Roman life, sea voyages, exotic African animals and lady athletes (the so-called bikini girls) is truly spine-tingling, transporting the viewer to a world so removed from our own.

“We believe this was a summer residence for a wealthy man,” says Rosalia. “The property is divided into several parts. There are the owner’s private apartments, an area for guests, a gymnasium, a banqueting hall and thermal baths which were open to the public.”

DAY SIX | Under the volcano | Taormina + Mount Etna

After the sensory and intellectual riches of the past five days, I’d imagined that the pace would slow down. How wrong could I be? The previous evening we’d driven to the medieval town of Taormina. A Sicilian version of Capri, this hilltop honeypot just oozes style, sophistication and money. An episode of The White Lotus was filmed at the Four Seasons Hotel here and at the town’s magnificent Teatro Greco.

Taormina, Mount Etna and the Ionian Sea from Piazza IX Aprile. iStock

Over the centuries Taormina has attracted European royalty, artists, movie stars and writers. D.H. Lawrence and his wife Frieda lived here for two years and I managed to track down his old house – now locked up – which has fine views over the Ionian Sea. “We love Taormina and in particular our house,” he wrote. “I love [watching] the sun rise over the open sea to the east.”

Visitors stroll through the pedestrianised main street of Taormina near to its city gate. iStock

Our lodging is called Hotel Splendid and shares the same jaw-dropping vista that Lawrence enjoyed. After breakfast, we’re off for a morning tour of Mount Etna, Europe’s highest (3327 metres) active volcano – its last eruptions were in 2001 and 2002.

The drive takes us up through vineyards, citrus orchards and neat little villages. The rich volcanic soil is responsible for the area’s abundance of cherries, hazelnuts, pears, strawberries, pistachios and, of course, grapes.

“A national park was established in 1987 which covers Mount Etna and also protects all the communities that exist on its slopes,” says Rosalia.

After pulling into the visitor centre, we spend a happy hour clambering around its bare, greyish slopes and photographing the moon-like craters. Our lunchtime stop is at Murgo Wines, one of 150 vineyards in the Mount Etna DOC, where we enjoy platters of cured meats, cheese and pickled vegetables and get to sample some estate wines, including a refreshing Etna rosso and an inky cabernet sauvignon from its Catania vineyards.

Gazing down over the plains below us this seems like the perfect place to say farewell to Sicily, but we have a full afternoon of sightseeing in Taormina before us. After seven days on the road, we’re still eager to see more.

Five more things to see and do in Sicily

Escape to the Aeolian Islands

Older Sicilians go all misty eyed at the mention of the Aeolian Islands. Known locally as the Seven Sisters, the archipelago off the north-eastern tip of Sicily has been a favourite holiday haunt for decades. Volcano Island, the closest to Sicily, offers the rare chance to hike on an active volcano plus taking a soak in the island’s health-giving thermal springs.

Sicily’s most charming village

Sick of fighting the crowds in Taormina? Then head up the hill to the medieval village of Castelmola. Built around a ruined Norman castle, the village is remarkably unspoilt, with picturesque terrace houses, narrow alleyways and several ancient churches. Visitors who hike the five kilometres from Taormina are rewarded with sweeping views of Mount Etna and the Straits of Messina.

Enna: A city in the sky

At 931 metres, Enna is Italy’s highest provincial city and one packed with ancient monuments and archaeological sites. Known as “the navel of Sicily” Enna is a stunning mountain town but attracts few tourists because of its remote location. Over the centuries, Enna has been ruled by the Greeks, the Romans, the Byzantines, the Arabs and the Normans who have all left their mark. Its many attractions include Italy’s largest medieval castle (Castello di Lombardia), a 14th century cathedral, and a temple site dedicated to Demeter. It also stages several dramatic religious festivals, including Madonna of the Visitation.

Hike Cavagrande del Cassibile

Cavagrande del Cassibile is a nature reserve near the towns of Avola, Noto, and Syracuse. Keen walkers can join a guided hike along a 10-kilometre stretch of the Cassibile River. The path passes through canyons and scrub and ends at the Cavagrande lakes. Other attractions include the necropolis of Cassibile, an archaeological site boasting a large system of caves and tunnels.

The world’s most beautiful city

Destroyed by a 1693 earthquake, Scicli was rebuilt in Baroque style. The writer Elio Vittorini described the resultant civic masterwork, 25 kilometres south of Ragusa, as perhaps “the most beautiful city in the world”. Today’s visitors to the town enjoy a wealth of ecclesiastic architecture, fine boulevards and imposing town squares set in a dramatic gorge.

THE DETAILS

TOUR

World.title: The other Australian Wolverine: Liam McIntyre on donning the adamantium claws
World.content:
TechnologyVideo games The other Australian Wolverine: Liam McIntyre on donning the adamantium claws Tim Biggs August 23, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than 25 years after Hugh Jackman first portrayed the character, another Australian actor is stepping into the yellow armour of one of Marvel’s most violent and most popular heroes. Liam McIntyre, 44, stars in Sony’s upcoming video game Marvel’s Wolverine, developed by Insomniac Games, creators of three highly acclaimed Spider-Man games. This new take on the character is bloody and action-packed, but has a complex emotional narrative at its core. A new PlayStation video game follows Wolverine as mutants and humanity clash for the first time. Set in a world where the X-Men don’t exist, and few people are even aware there are super-powered mutants among them, the game puts Logan — a practically indestructible mutant with retractable claws, traumatised by flashes of a past he can’t remember — in a power struggle between human and mutant factions who each want to eradicate the other’s species.



While there’s plenty of screaming and growling from McIntyre, his portrayal is more grounded and open than most. Still, as the character remains canonically Canadian, it begs the question; why do we keep seeing Australians in the role? “Australians don’t have a lot of self-importance. Tall poppy syndrome, help your mates out, that sort of thing,” said Mcintyre, in Melbourne to promote the game. “Wolverine is an unassuming, get-things-done kind of gruff, rugged [character]. I think his ethos aligns with what a lot of Australians view as some of the best qualities about ourselves. Maybe through that worldview, Australians are like, ‘I kind of think I get this guy’.” Liam McIntyre plays the unstoppable mutant in Marvel’s Wolverine. Despite Wolverine being a mutant, many stories feature him as a relatable, sympathetic character constantly under pressure. His abilities give him a responsibility to help people, but his powers also make him a liability. His lethality and animal-like instincts frequently open him up to manipulation from villains, and he’s only too aware of the possibility he could hurt the people he cares about.



In the game, Logan leaps around the screen tearing enemies apart, with consecutive kills filling a rage meter that unlocks even quicker and more violent attacks, and lets him shrug off damage. But we also see the character in quieter situations, struggling to understand his purpose. “A lot of superheroes have special powers, they’re doing special things and saving people, whereas it’s almost a burden for Logan. He’s most useful when he’s a weapon, that’s when he can enact the most change. But the way that he enacts that change takes a heavy toll on him,” McIntyre said. “He’s not necessarily excited to go out and save the world. He doesn’t want fanfare. He doesn’t want to get his name up in lights as a hero.” The camera is a lot closer, and the action a lot bloodier, than in Insomniac’s previous Spider-man games. McIntyre, born in Adelaide, has been based in the US since he was cast in the lead role of the Spartacus TV series in 2012. Since then, he’s had brushes with super-heroism in The Flash TV show and an animated Justice League feature, and he’s had success in video games as JD Fenix in the Gears of War series. But his latest role feels particularly special because he’s a long-time fan of Wolverine, and he’s still adjusting to seeing his face on the character.



At a preview event for the game at Marvel Stadium, the signboards and screens around the ground were all lit up with promotional images of the character. Sony has introduced special edition PlayStation 5 consoles with Wolverine printed on them. And at Disney’s recent D23 event in California, Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige introduced a look at the game on stage. “He pointed straight at my face! He might not have known that, but I mean, even tangentially, that’s just the wildest,” McIntyre said. “I was watching X-Men: The Animated Series as a 13-year-old thinking, ‘That Wolverine dude is cool.’ And now I’m here. There are these moments in your life where you’re just like, I can’t believe that guy became this guy. Me. It seems impossible.” Editor's pick Video games May the choice be with you: The next great Star Wars story might be a game Acting for blockbuster video games is no longer necessarily just about providing your voice and face. In addition to sound booth work, McIntyre spent four years off-and-on recording performance capture — which minutely tracks facial as well as whole-body movements — alongside stunt people and a core group of co-stars portraying mutants Sabretooth, Mystique and Jean Grey, who he says have all become friends.



But it was performing opposite prolific video game actor Troy Baker, who McIntyre has known for a long time, that he cites as a highlight of the process. “To work with someone who is that good is such a joy. He’s so in the moment, so fresh ... You don’t get many jobs like this in a career, where you really feel like everybody’s trying to make something truly special.” Releasing on September 15, the game comes at a time when Marvel’s also beginning to pull the X-Men and mutants into its big screen efforts. A key character featured in the game was also just introduced to the Marvel Cinematic Universe in Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Troy Baker’s character in the game is Nathaniel Essex, who in the comics becomes the villain Mister Sinister, who was just announced at D23 as heading to the MCU portrayed by Adam Driver. While Insomniac could not have known any of this during development, the game’s senior project director Jess Reiner-Reed said that these characters have decades of history, and that fans are happy to see multiple versions of them at once as long as the stories are compelling and ring true. “Having exposure around all these different characters only enriches the universe. We can take inspiration from the movies and TV shows, and they take some inspiration from us,” she said, referring to the well-documented impact of the Spider-Man video games on Brand New Day’s choreography and effects.



“Audiences trust the care we put into these uniquely Insomniac stories, and they can trust that we’re going to do the same thing with Wolverine.” Get news and reviews on technology, gadgets and gaming in our Technology newsletter every Friday. Sign up here.

World.title: High rents a roadblock to productivity
World.content:
NationalNSWRenting Editorial High rents a roadblock to productivity The Herald's View Editorial August 23, 2026 — 6:00am

August 23, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The interests of renters are often treated as a footnote in Sydney’s never-ending conversation about property prices. But even with the recent dip in house prices, buying a property remains out of reach for many – especially buying a home that is within reasonable reach of the workplace. Rents are high in central Sydney. Dominic Lorrimer New data revealed in The Sun-Herald today shows there has been little respite from rental rises across Sydney, with the price of owning your own home keeping large numbers of people in the rental market, especially in the inner cities where they compete with international students to lease apartments. Senior economics correspondent Shane Wright reports that in some parts of the country, rents have risen by 80 per cent since the COVID-era rent freeze.



In Zetland, Chippendale and Haymarket in inner Sydney, rents have jumped by between $367 and $452 a week, Wright reports. The picture is mixed, though, with some Sydney suburbs – such as Hunters Hill, Avalon Beach and Hornsby Heights – recording rental price growth slower than the city’s 23.6 per cent inflation rate since mid-2021. The NSW South Coast has bucked the national trend, with landlords in some towns asking less on average than they were in 2021. These falls are attributed to less demand since the COVID-era surge of people seeking to leave Sydney and Canberra. Effects of the current house price slump on the rental market are unclear, but in theory the slump may enable more renters to become home owners, which in turn would ease price pressure in the broader rental market.



There are many other factors at play, though, including federal changes to negative gearing that some fear will force landlords to lift rents to compensate for their lost tax breaks. Related Article Renting Rents spike up to 80 per cent as people are pushed from houses to units The national data that Wright reports on today suggests local factors – including proximity to major employment and education zones, transport and the regional cost of living – heavily influence how much landlords can charge. The most obvious remedy is to increase housing supply in areas where people want to live. In Sydney, the Minns government has taken steps in the right direction with its overhaul of the planning system and focus on transport-oriented development.



Higher densities are a central mechanism for solving the housing crisis for renters and home owners alike. Related Article Analysis

Home loans Five charts that explain what’s really happening with housing It is true that existing high-density areas of Sydney have been home to some of the nation’s biggest rent rises since COVID. But as more high-rise development takes place in well-located areas of the city, tenants will have more options and landlords can be expected to curb rent rises to attract them. Landlords need a fair return on their investment. But affordable housing lifts overall living standards and can benefit the wider economy, as people are able to spend more of their money on things other than housing.



Young people especially can be caught in the trap of paying high rents and being unable to save a deposit to get their feet on the first rungs of the property ladder. Everyone deserves a place to call home, and the end goal for policymakers must balance the needs of investors with equitable outcomes for ordinary residents of NSW. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Heather and Hugo met at drama school 40 years ago. They haven’t stopped working together since
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There is a familiarity within the Australian creative scene that gives audiences a unique kinship with the actors who appear on our screens and stages. These are the faces we have grown up with, who we have aged with, and who we innately feel like — were we to run into them at the pub — we could share a beer with. It gives our home-grown productions a warm, fuzzy feeling because, not only do we recognise familiar streets, landmarks and cafes used as filming locations, but we feel an instant intimacy when recognisable faces appear. The pride is palpable. Occasionally, a production comes along that is so successful in creating that feeling of familiarity you can’t help but smile when you watch it, even if the subject makes you cry or shift uncomfortably in your seat. And that, in a nutshell, is Dalliance. Hugo Weaving and Heather Mitchell in Dalliance. The good friends have worked together for more than 40 years. The six-episode drama series charts the fallout from one big, life-changing event and the ways it radically upends a group of 60-something friends. Exploring everything from female friendship and the path to parenthood to sex, desire and ambition, it’s the latest endeavour from John and Dan Edwards, the father-and-son production duo behind Bump and The F Ward. The series also marks a reunion for long-time friends and collaborators Heather Mitchell and Hugo Weaving, who star as would-be romantic interests, Dani and Billy. Their on-screen rapport is instant, but when you’ve shared stage and screen for over 40 years, that’s to be expected. Related Article Review What to stream this week: A juicy holiday-from-hell Brit drama, plus five more picks “I feel so blessed every time I get to work with him,” Mitchell says of her decades-long friend. “From when we first worked together … there’s always been a lot of laughter, a lot of fun and ease. It hasn’t changed, really, over the years. And that’s the thing about getting older. [With] people you’ve known for a long time, you sort of slot right back to where you were.”



The pair first met at the prestigious National Institute of Dramatic Art (NIDA) in 1979, began working together at Sydney Theatre Company in 1982, and, most recently, shared the screen in Binge’s acclaimed multi-generational drama Love Me. “I adore Heather,” says Weaving. “Working with her is being embraced. She has a capacity to care about others like no one else and I consider myself hugely lucky to get to play with her whenever we work together.” Georgie Parker as Rose, Hugo Weaving as Billy, and Heather Mitchell as Dani in Dalliance. Dalliance is a reunion for many of the cast, and remarkable in that most of them are in their 50s and 60s. Mitchell was most excited by the prospect of giving talented friends, such as Catherine McClements, an opportunity to expand their creative horizons. “I loved watching her play a character who’s sexy, funny and complex when she’s so often cast as brittle and tough.” She also knew the perfect person for the role of Rose, Billy’s wife of 40 years, pleading with Home and Away producer Julie McGauran to release Georgie Parker, who has spent 16 years working on the soap, for Dalliance. “I’ve known Georgie Parker since we were in our 20s, and I think this role shows people the depth of her talent.” Related Article Australian TV This TV legend has guided us through every decade of life. Next up? Our 60s By nature of the series’ time-jumping format, Weaving worked mostly with Mitchell and David Wenham, who plays Billy’s volatile younger brother, but relished the chance to connect with old friends. “Our read-through days were very special, all the cast together for two days. It was so lovely to catch up with everyone.” And like all great 21st-century friendships, Mitchell adds, the WhatsApp group is still going strong. “We’re constantly writing to each other on because we formed such a close relationship between all of us. It’s beautiful.”



For 68-year-old Mitchell, this was a project particularly close to her heart. Despite a career rich with experience (she won her second AACTA Award in February for The Narrow Road to the Deep North), this is her first time in the producer’s seat. She was quick to accept when John Edwards made the offer. “One of the beautiful things about being older is the challenges are less risky because you’ve got less to lose, if that makes sense.” “And I have loved it,” she adds, pointing out that her age gave her the confidence to ask questions. “I haven’t beaten myself up if I don’t know something. I just say, ‘Can you help me with this?’ I’d go to the production manager and say, ‘I have no idea what this means.’ I think as I’m getting older, I ask for help more.” Georgie Parker as Rose and David Wenham as Gary in Dalliance. Camaraderie played a pivotal role in not only the chemistry between the actors and behind the scenes – Mitchell’s husband of 34 years, Martin McGrath, is the show’s director of photography – but also in the writing room, where lived experience and a willingness to be vulnerable gave depth to each character’s journey. Related Article Opinion

Australian TV If you are still complaining about Australian TV, it’s time to shut up Louise Rugendyke National TV editor “We talked a lot about sexuality,” says Mitchell. “Passion, love, sex. People who’ve been through cancer, how medication affects your sexuality, how desire changes for each person as they get older. Some people just do not want to be touched any more. Other people long for it desperately. For me personally, I’m probably saying too much … [but] I’m more sexually satisfied in my 60s than I ever have been. And I know what I want. “We really wanted to explore both men and women and whatever gender, that there is no time limit to love and companionship and sex. And that sex is not the driving thing for everybody. That often people go online looking for very different things. And sometimes it is sex with no other attachments. And other times, someone is really looking for a true love. The past can turn up.



“So we talked at length about what is sexuality, and how is it perceived? And I would hope that for younger people, if any younger people watch this show, that they will also feel that life doesn’t stop. You don’t stop growing. You don’t stop living. You don’t stop wanting.” Mitchell and Weaving in the 1984 miniseries Bodyline. It was the first time they played partners on screen. Dalliance, and Mitchell’s own sharpened focus on life, touches on what psychologists call “socioemotional selectivity theory”. It argues that we shift our priorities and goals depending on how long we think we have left. Young people who see the future as long and open-ended prioritise knowledge and building their social network, while those further along in life, faced with their own mortality, grow more selective. They chase emotionally meaningful goals, avoid obvious risk, and prioritise close relationships over new connections. “The older you get, you’re looking closer to the idea of death. More friends die around you, more things happen which you might feel will result in an ending,” reflects Mitchell. “Certainly within this show, we want to say, no one’s ready to end anything. These characters aren’t thinking of endings, they’re thinking of beginnings, like how do I want to live the rest of my life? How do I want to be with the people I love?” Loading Endings, as it happens, are fresh in Mitchell’s mind. She recently starred in black comedy The Fox, which would become one of the late Sam Neill’s final roles (though with Neill as the voice of a magpie, they didn’t actually share the screen). “Sam was a very, very dear friend of mine,” says Mitchell, who also paid tribute to Neill at the recent Logie Awards. “I’ve spent a lot of time with him, and my husband was a close friend of Sam’s. He’s directed me, I’ve acted with him, but our main relationship is a non-professional one – I actually went out with him when I was 22 – and I still feel his presence enormously. “And there again, a man in his late 70s who was working and had jobs lined up.
