So much of his identity and his love was in his work, the people and the industry. I think it’s important for people to know, he was not a weakened person. He was strong right up until the end.”

World.title: Labour releases fiscal strategy, promises to slash debt
World.content:
Labour has released their fiscal strategy for the election, promising to get back to surplus by 2029/30, slash debt and set up an independent Parliamentary Budget Office, if elected.

Leader Chris Hipkins said his party would "get the books back into shape", but would not do it by "making life harder" and cutting services.

"New Zealand should be a country where hard work gets you somewhere. Where you can get ahead, put down roots and know your kids will have opportunities here.

"We'll invest in the things that make New Zealand stronger - our hospitals and schools, infrastructure, skills and the businesses that create jobs" Hipkins said.

Labour's fiscal strategy has six policies:

Achieve a surplus by 2029/30 and keep a sustainable fiscal position over the forecast period. Labour return to using the original OBEGAL (Operating Balance Before Gains and Losses) indicator and ditch the OBEGALx measure introduced by Finance Minister Nicola Willis.

Aim to reduce net debt down to 20 percent of GDP over time and investment in initiatives that support a growing economy.

Keep core Crown Expenditure and revenue at around 33 percent of GDP when their capital gains tax is fully implemented.

Set up an independent Parliamentary Budget Office to scrutinise government finances and election commitments.

Give the Reserve Bank it's dual mandate back, making so it must consider price stability and maximum sustainable employment.

And, bring back wellbeing reporting to so decisions take into account the impact on New Zealanders.

Finance and economy spokesperson Barbara Edmonds said the plan would balance the books and bring down debt, while giving New Zealand the "capacity to invest in its future".

"Labour will return the books to surplus by 2029/30 and reduce net debt over time but we won't do that by cutting the foundations of our economy."

Finance and economy spokesperson Barbara Edmonds and Labour leader Chris Hipkins. Baz Macdonald/RNZ

"Under National unemployment is at an 11-year high, business liquidations are up 71 percent, homelessness and KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals are at record levels, and public services are under pressure - that isn't economic success," Edmonds said.

It comes two weeks after the National Party released its own so-called Budget Responsibility Rules which Finance spokesperson Nicola Willis described as "fiscal guard-rails" and leader Christopher Luxon said would protect the country against economic shocks.

National said it would return to surplus in 2028/29 - under its OBEGALx formula - but would hit surplus the same year as Labour is projecting under the OBEGAL measure.

World.title: Hundreds across Wellington, South Island without power
World.content:
Hundreds of homes across Wellington and the South Island are without power this morning.

Wellington electricity reported outages for more than 1300 customers in the Naenae, Plimmerton, and Kaitoke areas.

Power Co said over 200 homes are without power in Carterton, and 150 in Taihape.

Network Tasman has recorded 1300 unplanned outages across the region.

About 80 homes in the Wahapo Area on the West Coast are without power, according to provider Westpower.

Orion says about 20 homes just out of Christchurch in the Little River area also have no power.

Meanwhile, a powerline has fallen and is hanging low across Treadwell Street in Lower Hutt.

World.title: How world media reacted to All Blacks win over South Africa
World.content:
The All Blacks have beaten the Springboks 33-16 in the opening Test of their tour of South Africa in Johannesburg.

New Zealand's win - by a rather significant margin of 17 points - was dubbed "surprising" and "comfortable", with world media highlighting the All Blacks dominating performance.

Meanwhile, the Springboks were left to reflect on a disappointing performance, as noted by media.

The victory gives the All Blacks an early advantage in the four-match series and will give the team a boost of confidence heading into the second Test.

Here's how world media reacted to the All Blacks vs Springboks series opener.

The Telegraph

The Telegraph's post-match article describes the All Blacks victory as a "statement win".

"Rugby's Greatest Rivalry did not begin with the year's greatest game, but a New Zealand victory against the odds, at high altitude in Johannesburg, has poured intrigue and interest on to a series which was already brimming with them," the article reads.

It said the All Blacks win was almost as "comfortable as it was surprising".

Rugby 365

"Wasteful" is how the online outlet Rugby 365 has described the Springboks performance.

The Boks wasted several scoring opportunities throughout the game, which couldn't be ignored.

The article said that "proved costly as New Zealand took their chances to outscore the hosts by five tries to one".

Will Jordan scores a try. Photosport NZ Ltd / www.photosport.nz

RugbyPass

Online outlet RugbyPass' post-match article angles in on All Black Will Jordan, who said the victory "means everything".

"Serious shift of 80 minutes, love the way our boys just dug deep. Some guys playing here against the Springboks for the first time, got a taste of what it's like.

"Extremely proud of our whole group. We realise it's just one of four, but an awesome start to us for the series."

The article highlights that despite the win, the group understood it was the first Test of a four-match series.

The South African

"All Blacks punish Springboks" - a line from The South African newspaper.

The paper's post-match article focuses on the Springboks losing their World Rugby No 1 ranking.

"The result not only gives the All Blacks the early advantage in the four-Test Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series, but also sees them move above South Africa at the summit of the world rankings," the online paper wrote.

It noted that the 17-point victory was New Zealand's biggest-ever win over the Springboks at Ellis Park in South Africa.

World.title: Exit interview with Labour's Duncan Webb
World.content:
As the final few weeks of the 54th Parliament approach, the House enters valedictory season, a period when MPs pause briefly to give their retiring colleagues a chance to say farewell.

House on Sunday: Duncan Webb exit interview The House Download MP3 11m

The first MP since May to say haere rā and hang up his boots - or rather his trademark Labour-red Swanndri - is Dr Duncan Webb, MP for Christchurch Central.

Throughout Webb's nine-year tenure, he's had a go at just about every role Parliament has to offer; serving on numerous committees (some of which he chaired), a stint as a minister, as both junior and senior whip, as well as taking an array of spokesperson roles.

He's a stalwart of the late night committee stage, and good for a solid filibuster. He has been something of an enduring presence in the debating chamber, clocking up long hours on his feet, speaking in a characteristically conversational barrister style.

Rather than simply regurgitate a transcript of his valedictory speech which you can watch here on Parliament's website, The House sat down with Webb for an exit interview.

We reflected on his time in Parliament as an active practitioner of parliamentary process, a reliable source of structured argument and, often, a recognisable hearty chuckle.

Duncan Webb makes his valedictory speech VNP/Louis Collins

Webb told me his background as a lawyer didn't quite prepare him for the realities of Parliament, where much of the work relies on maintaining relationships and familiarising yourself with an esoteric set of unwritten rules.

He particularly enjoyed his time as Chief Whip, describing the role as one where he could work behind the scenes to help the party get things done-without necessarily being in the headlines.

But it was the minutiae of parliamentary procedure where he was arguably most in his element, especially during this current parliamentary term.

Whether reaching back into the muscle memory of litigation for select committee scrutiny, or relishing the late-night debates, votes and the occasional opportunity to catch the government short on numbers, Webb said he enjoyed paying attention and catching mistakes.

Like many departing MPs he did have reflections about the way the House operates.

Webb argued that legislation was too often being pushed through late at night when MPs were exhausted, and that select committees were being asked to handle too much work.

He also believed ministers should be held to a higher standard when answering questions in the House during Question Time.

After nine years, though, Webb reckoned the time was right to call it a day.

The possibility of him returning to government as a Justice Minister if Labour were to win the next election isn't enough of a temptation to change his mind.

Three more years, the Christchurch Central MP said, might chip away at the "cheerful, happy disposition" he currently held.

For now, he enjoyed the final weeks: no portfolios, no major responsibilities; just lending his colleagues his expertise in policy and debate and, as he puts it, "just helping everyone out."

You can listen to The House's chat with Dr Duncan Webb by clicking the link near the top of the page.

World.title: Government to retain Labour's clean car standard for imported high-emissions vehicles
World.content:
The government will retain a clean car standard that charges importers a fee for bringing high-emissions vehicles into the country.

However, it has not yet decided on the new limits that will be in force, saying it will work with the motor industry to develop settings that are "realistic and achievable".

Introduced by the previous government, the Clean Vehicle Standard charges importers a penalty for cars that exceed the target emissions level, but that can be offset by also importing cars with lower emissions.

Transport Minister Chris Bishop slashed the penalty by nearly 80 percent last November, saying supply constraints meant importers could not source enough low-emissions vehicles to avoid being penalised.

That could result in buyers paying thousands of dollars extra, Bishop said at the time.

Earlier this year, he launched a full review of the standard, which included an option to scrap it altogether.

That would have made New Zealand one of just two OECD countries to not have a vehicle emissions standard - the other is Russia.

Clean car advocates warned at the time that loosening the limits, or scrapping them altogether, would result in New Zealand being sold the high-emitting leftovers that manufacturers could no longer sell in Australia.

Australia introduced its own limits late last year, with the first six months of data showing overall tailpipe emissions had dropped and most importers were able to meet the standard.

Bishop said the decision to slash the standard last year was critical to ease pressure on importers and keep cars affordable.

However, the review had found the standard was "the most cost-effective way to increase the availability of lower-emissions vehicles in New Zealand", he said on Friday.

Most of the motor industry supported retaining some version of the standard, he said.

"In feedback on the review, industry noted that the standard is now well established in New Zealand, with importers accumulating credits and charges over time. Removing it at this stage would be highly disruptive for the vehicle industry."

The government would now go ahead with the next stage of the review, "to calibrate the settings so they are realistic and achievable for industry", Bishop said.

"The government has also agreed to set different targets for used vehicle imports to reflect that they have different and older technology."

Officials would report back early in 2027, and new targets and settings would take effect from 1 January, 2028.

A spokesperson for Bishop confirmed that the current settings would stay in place until then.

World.title: The House: Government inaction undermines early cancer diagnosis and treatment
World.content:
MPs have been asked to pressure the government, in the hope it will use an existing law to protect insurance consumers from genomic discrimination.

Professor Andrew Shelling, an Auckland University cancer researcher and a leader of Against Genomic Discrimination Aotearoa (AGenDA), told the health committee that insurance misuse of DNA data was discouraging testing, which "undermines prevention, early diagnosis, family testing, genomic research and clinical childhood treatment".

Government DNA inaction undermining prevention, diagnosis and treatment. The House Download MP3 5m

The Contracts of Insurance Act 2024 received royal assent in November 2024, after years of development. Among its fixes, it empowers the minister of health to regulate against insurance companies demanding DNA tests or using genomic data to decide premiums or coverage.

No regulations have been written to effect such changes and AGenDA says no action has been taken by the government to enable those regulations.

Fay Sowerby, also from AGenDA, said: "Delay is a significant public health issue."

She pointed out that, within the OECD, New Zealand was at the far end - with Columbia and Costa Rica - being "without operative protection, [in] governing insurers use of predictive genetic test results".

"This is not theoretical," Sowerby said. "A New Zealand woman with a BRCA 2 variant reports paying premium, subject to a 50 percent loading for 15 years, despite risk-reducing surgery.

"Her daughter was quoted as 75 percent loading, despite testing negative for the familial variant. The cases reveal a one-way ratchet.

"Adverse results can increase premiums or restrict cover, while negative results and risk-reducing interventions may receive little favourable weight."

There are two barriers to regulation taking effect.

Before any regulations can be recommended, the act requires the minister of health to engage in consultation with both the Financial Markets Authority and those the minister considers may be substantially affected.

After two years, apparently no consultation had been undertaken. This week's calls were for the start of the consultation process.

A further roadblock has been the act's unusually nebulous commencement date. The whole act - or its parts - can come into effect by Order in Council or, if not, they automatically take effect when three years have passed since the royal assent.

"That very long delay comes to an end in November 2027. AGenDA wants consultation to begin this year, so regulations can be ready to go, when the bill reaches its default date for coming into effect.

The genetic testing component (or any part of the act) could come into force before that date, if the government was to recommend to the governor-general that it do so.

This part of the act received cross-party support when it was debated, so MPs from across the House asked what reason AGenDa had been given for the lack of progress.

Sowerby told them: "The only comment we've had is 'prioritisation'."

World.title: Firefighters investigating cause of large Wānaka blaze
World.content:
Firefighters are investigating the cause of a ferocious fire that blazed through trees and scrub in Wānaka, sending flames leaping metres into the air and forced the evacuation of 22 homes.

The blaze broke out near Lagoon Avenue at 7.30pm on Saturday night and tore through steep hillsides close to houses, fanned by strong winds.

Fire and Emergency said no houses had caught fire on Saturday, although emergency services initially thought seven to eight properties were under threat.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) crews brought the flames under control using eight trucks and three support vehicles, but were still dealing with hotspots, flare-ups and flying embers late into the night.

In McLellan Place, Marty Lohrey said he had been shocked to open the curtains to see flames tearing through kānuka behind his house.

"Very quickly they just flared up, within a few moments, probably 10-20 metres in the air. Quite quickly the wind just whipped them down the terrace. It was really hot, noisy, and all the embers were blowing across the houses. It made you think of the forest fires we've seen, everyone was pretty scared," he said.

Lohrey said neighbours were knocking on each other's doors and calling 111.

Firefighters have been working to put out a large fire in the Wānaka suburb of Albert Town that earlier threatened houses, and expect to be there into Sunday morning. RNZ/ Katie Todd

"I think we've dodged a bullet because there's no property damage. The fire boys were all here pretty quickly. The response by the fire brigade and police has been fantastic," he said.

Corey Young said he saw a bright glow in the sky from his living room and raced out to help the firefighters.

"They got on top of it pretty quickly but it was very, very close to a number of houses, it was pretty scary actually," he said.

"It was looking pretty grim there for a little bit until they arrived on the scene.

"I could feel the heat from the fire. Some of the flames got probably a good 20 metres high at times. It was just making sure that the people in those houses were safe."

Young said people were ready to use garden hoses and buckets of spa pool water to try to protect their properties.

"It was pretty touch and go there. There was smoke billowing everywhere," he said.

Hunt Place resident Del Tubb told RNZ the fire started with a roar: "[We] looked out the window and it was like a blazing inferno right across the garden. Everything was bright red and there were embers. It was pretty scary stuff," he said.

He quickly grabbed warm clothes to go out into the night and moved two cars. Talking on Saturday night he was relieved a woodshed just over the fence from the flames had not gone up in flames.

Strong winds and fire a bad mix, firefighter says

Fire and Emergency NZ Queenstown Lakes manager Nic McQuillan in Albert Town, on Saturday night. RNZ/ Katie Todd

FENZ assistant district commander Nic McQuillan told RNZ that dry, windy weather was problematic, even in winter.

"We don't know how the fire started but I would just ask people to be conscious of the fact that even though it's still coming out of winter, everything is dry, the wind is a real problem when it comes to a spark or an ember that gets out of control," he said

McQuillan said people getting rid of ashes from fires should make sure they are completely cool before disposing of them and check if conditions are safe before lighting a fire.

World.title: Hospital security appeared powerless against 'intimidating' patient, witness says
World.content:
A woman who waited more than eight hours in a hospital emergency department says security officers appeared powerless to stop a man intimidating other patients.

The woman, who asked not to be named, arrived at the Palmerston North Hospital ED about 3pm on 28 July.

The man was escorted in by police about 11pm, who then left the scene, she said. The man behaved poorly, getting in people's faces, vaping, crashing into a wall and writhing on the ground, she said.

The man appeared to have come to the emergency department because of a sore shoulder, she said.

"He was just being really weird and intimidating, and walking up to people and staring at them in the eyes, then walking on to the next person.

"There were a number of older people and people with little babies in there, and he didn't seem to care about that," she said.

He was physically intimidating due to his size, she added.

"Everyone was just avoiding this guy's gaze, really, like you would if you had a scary dog."

The woman said two or three security officers were keeping an eye on the man, but were not intervening.

At present they can only calm situations without using force.

Emergency Department security guards deal with increase in physical and verbal abuse Morning Report Download MP3 5m

"He just felt like someone who at any point could give someone a big whack on the head. He was also really out of it," the woman told RNZ.

"It was just really surprising to me that anyone like that was allowed to stay in that space and they weren't asked to leave."

The man was there for about 30 minutes before he went to the department desk and demanded to be seen. Despite many others having waited for hours, the man was attended to by medical staff.

"I really felt for the medical team, because it was like, 'let's just get this guy out of the way, this volatile person, and let's just treat him'.

"But that just creates this sort of feeling that you come in, you behave terribly, you're intimidating, and then you get looked after. Meanwhile, there are other people who are patiently waiting."

The woman said she would like to see hospital security given more power to remove people from hospital property when they behave as the man did.

RNZ has previously reported calls for beefed up powers for security officers amid growing instances of violence and intimidation at hospitals, although some in the health sector say such moves could be problematic.

The Post reported this week that Heath NZ is planning on spending up to $100 million on improved security in hospitals.

Health NZ says security staff and clinical teams are trained in calming and de-escalation techniques. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Poor behaviour not tolerated - Health NZ

RNZ contacted Health NZ about the incident. Included in our questions was what should happen in such situations, was this incident reported by staff and had officials considered giving hospital security more powers.

Health NZ's interim group director of operations for MidCentral, Katherine Fraser-Chapple, said patient safety was the organisation's highest priority.

"We want everyone who attends Palmerston North Hospital to feel safe and supported while receiving care," she said.

"We do not tolerate behaviour that causes distress, intimidation or risk to patients, visitors, or staff.

"Health New Zealand has processes in place to manage disruptive or concerning behaviour, including support from security staff and clinical teams trained in calming and de-escalation techniques."

Fraser-Chapple said where appropriate, security staff would work alongside police "to help maintain a safe environment for everyone in our care".

World.title: The archer who shoots a target he cannot see
World.content:
As James Griffiths draws his bow, he steadies his breath and aims at a target he cannot see.

Mr Griffiths is a newcomer to vision-impaired archery after a Type 2 diabetes diagnosis cost him much of his vision.

Now, he relies on touch, sound and trust to ensure his aim is true.

But the 46-year-old from Sale in Victoria's east is targeting more than just a bullseye when he picks up a bow.

"When they say you can't do this and you can't do that, I will prove people wrong," Mr Griffiths said.

"[We're told] blind people aren't supposed to do this … why not? Why shouldn't we?"

James Griffiths wants to show that people with disability can achieve their goals, no matter the obstacles they may encounter. (ABC News: Lily Kristanto)

Mr Griffiths discovered archery through a "come and try" session promoted by Gippsland Disability Advocacy Incorporated.

It didn't take long for him to be hooked.

"I can shoot at a target I can't see, and the only person I'm competing against is myself," he said.

He is now working towards the World Archery Para Championships while holding onto the dream of becoming a Paralympian — if vision-impaired (VI) archery is one day added to the games.

How vision-impaired archery works

Mr Griffiths uses his cane to familiarise himself with the range before aiming with a tactile sight that rests against the back of his hand.

He also wears blackout glasses while shooting, designed to block out any remaining vision and ensure all VI archers compete on a level playing field.

After each shot, Mr Griffiths' support worker uses a spotting scope to locate where the arrows have hit.

Before shooting, James Griffiths uses his cane to practice his positioning and familiarise himself with the direction of his bow towards the target. (ABC News: Jack Colantuono)

The target is described like the face of an analogue clock, with his support worker relaying a specific "time" back to him.

It allows him to build a mental picture of the target, whilst also listening to hear if his shot hit the target.

James Griffiths wears blackout glasses when participating in archery. (ABC News: Lily Kristanto)

Peter Bennett, president of the Twin City Archers in Morwell, said Mr Griffiths is a tenacious and determined athlete.

"The challenge is you've got no relationship to the target," Mr Bennett said.

" So he's got to feel for it and listen to the people around him that are helping him get there. "

Mr Griffiths is the first vision-impaired archer Mr Bennett has trained and one of around a dozen or so competitors nationally.

"There's not a big amount yet, but they're getting there; It's growing," Mr Bennett said.

James Griffiths discusses his technique with coach Peter Bennett at Twin City Archers in Morwell. (ABC News: Lily Kristanto)

Health battle

Mr Griffiths' journey to the archery range followed years of health challenges.

He was diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes at 19 before complications from the condition affected his eyesight and kidneys, eventually leading to a kidney-pancreas transplant that saved his life.

Mr Griffiths said his illness forced him into early retirement and that his experience has driven him to encourage others to take their health seriously.

"Diabetes is not a joke," he said.

" I'm lucky I've only gone blind from diabetes ... but other people lose their hands, their feet, their legs, their life. "

Peter Bennett says Mr Griffiths is the first vision-impaired archer he has trained at his club. (ABC News: Lily Kristanto)

Mr Bennett said Mr Griffiths has already shown the commitment needed to pursue the sport.

"He's got a good attitude; he's come in here, he has some goals that he wants to achieve and he's quite happy to put the work in to get there, which is great, that's what you need," he said.

"He's achieved a lot, his scores are going up, and so far the scores he's shot are doing very well in Australia ranking-wise."

The para-archer said he hoped to make his granddaughter proud by competing in archery competitions around the world.

"She's absolutely beautiful, full of beans, full of energy, loves to run around, yell, scream, sing, everything," Mr Griffiths said.

He wanted his journey to encourage others living with disability to try something new.

Every arrow tells a story, with James Griffiths relying on touch, sound and his team’s guidance to build a picture of where each shot lands. (ABC News: Lily Kristanto)

"If you find a sport you're interested in, just see if they can modify it to help you," he said.

"The guys here are absolutely great … wonderful people, really helpful, patient, great advice."

World.title: Norris to start on pole for Dutch GP as Russell claims sprint
World.content:
Lando Norris found unexpected pace to beat his rivals and the weather to take pole position for the Dutch Grand Prix after George Russell took a sprint race win on Formula 1's return from its mid-season break.

As rain started to fall on the Zandvoort track, McLaren's Norris made the most of his final run to reclaim pole by 0.102 of a second from Russell, whose Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli — the standings leader — was third.

Australia's Oscar Piastri will start fourth, having finished fifth in the sprint.

"A little surprised, honestly, but a decent lap," said Norris, who had been critical of his car in the earlier sprint race and credited McLaren with making the right changes.

"We had to try something because what we had before wasn't going to be enough," he said, adding the changes were small but "enough to give me some confidence."

Norris won the last race in Hungary on July 26 but was deflated after the sprint, saying McLaren wasn't competitive at all in slower corners.

Russell is rebuilding his title challenge after losing ground to Antonelli last month and said it was "a real joy" to drive in qualifying. The plan now is to "get in my groove again and try to fight with them tomorrow," he added.

Lewis Hamilton lost ground to Antonelli in the standings in the sprint race. His difficult day continued with fifth in qualifying.

The sprint race was a display of domination from Russell, who started from pole position, quickly built a gap to Norris in second and managed the pace from there, taking his first win since the Austrian Grand Prix in June.

"Obviously a great start to the weekend," he said.

Charles Leclerc snatched second off Norris with a daring pass into the inside of the first corner with six laps to go, but couldn't get close enough to try passing Russell.

Norris held off a late charge from Antonelli to stay third as the Italian pulled out of a potential overtaking move on the final lap.

"We just don't have the pace in general, especially in the slow-speed corners," Norris said.

Fourth-place Antonelli, starting fifth after car damage in qualifying, still managed to extend his standings lead by three more points to 53 because Hamilton could only manage seventh for Ferrari.

F1 still hasn't had a wet race this year but came tantalisingly close as rain fell as the drivers were heading back to the pits, seconds after the sprint finished.

"If there was one more lap it would have been a very, potentially, different end to the race so I'm glad the rain came when it did," Russell said.

While it stayed dry, overtaking was difficult, even in a year where the cars' electrical power has made back-and-forth passes common. The overtakes by Leclerc and Antonelli were the only changes of position anywhere in the top 11 finishers.

World.title: 'We're all gonna make it': What gymbros are getting wrong about Zyzz
World.content:
For a certain generation of Australian men, the path to the gym began with a photograph of a shirtless young man from Sydney.

His videos were brash, his poses were deliberately ridiculous, and at times he said deliberately provocative and offensive things to garner attention.

His catchphrases spread through bodybuilding forums, YouTube and social media, and some are now resurfacing as a new documentary hits our screens about one of Australia's earliest social media celebrities.

Aziz Shavershian had the muscles, the tan, the hair and the confidence, and he is the subject of Stan's new film, Poster Boy: Becoming Zyzz.

Zyzz was one of Australia's earliest social media celebrities. (Supplied: Stan)

But for all this renewed attention, Aziz won't hear or see it, having died in Thailand at just 22 years of age in 2011.

Fifteen years after his death, Aziz, known by his online moniker Zyzz, has become part of a new wave of online content celebrating an earlier era of gym and rave culture.

But it also comes at a time when a new generation is encouraged to pursue physical perfection through so-called looksmaxxing by a slightly amorphous online world of male influencers pushing misogyny broadly referred to as the manosphere.

Psychologist sounds alarm over looksmaxxing While it's a bit of fun for some, the social media trend known as looksmaxxing can have major impacts on young men's physical and mental health.

It is a strange moment to watch for his older brother, Said Shavershian, also known as ChestBrah.

He said the culture around young men's bodies and masculinity now looks very different from the one he and Aziz helped create.

"What me and Aziz always preached was: 'We're all going to make it,'" he said.

"It's a message of just that, 'Hey man, if I made it, so can you.' And that was what we're always about, just uplifting the little guy and uplifting anyone to be the master of their destiny."

Before Tate, there was Zyzz

Andrew and Tristan Tate are now among the world's most recognisable figures in the online manosphere, building enormous audiences around a highly performative version of masculinity, wealth and status.

The brothers are currently in custody in the United States as the British government tries to extradite them to face charges of rape, assault and facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation.

Why the Tate brothers were arrested Everything you need to know about the arrest of the Tate brothers.

In Poster Boy, it is put to the audience that the blueprint for the modern male influencer was being tested years earlier in Sydney, with Zyzz at the head of an "aesthetics movement".

But Said does not see the Tates as inheritors of his brother's message or good representations of masculinity.

For him, masculinity is something far less flashy than fast cars and fancy watches.

"Being someone that's vulnerable, that's kind, that's loving," he said.

"Young men out there, young boys don't really have many positive role models to look up to in society and ones they can kind of feel relatable to."

From Sydney gyms to the looksmaxxing era

Said Shavershian says he and his brother wanted to uplift young men. (Supplied: triple j)

Together, the brothers helped turn bodybuilding into something less about standing on a competition stage and more about being part of a lifestyle.

"Shredding for Stereosonic" became a cultural in-joke, and Aziz became its poster boy.

But the pursuit has become much more extreme online since the height of Zyzz, with communities obsessing over facial structure, perceived attractiveness and where an individual sits in a hierarchy of male beauty in what is known as looksmaxxing.

Said sees the connection and the merits in taking pride in your appearance, but said "deep, deep down, it's quite toxic".

He points to practices such as "face pulling" and "bone smashing" as examples of where the pursuit of physical perfection can go, with men ultimately ranking themselves against others.

The aesthetics movement appears to be a precursor to today's "looksmaxxing" phenomenon. (Supplied: Stan)

"With the digital age and social media, there's more information out there," he said.

"Anyone could just post anything, rage bait, any kind of content to kind of reel an audience in."

And once the algorithm finds an audience, it can keep serving them the same message, particularly targeting boys and young men at impressionable ages.

Documentary asks pertinent questions of peptides

Beyond its examination of modern masculinity, the film examines Zyzz's death and his use of steroids and peptides.

For years, the story repeated online was simple: the impossibly fit 22-year-old had suffered a heart attack in a Thai sauna.

The film reveals that Zyzz died from acute respiratory failure after taking a combination of morphine, cocaine and benzodiazepines.

He also had an enlarged heart, although the cause of that enlargement remains unclear.

Said Shavershian remembers Aziz as his "younger, goofy, dorky, highly intellectual brother". (ABC News)

There is no direct attribution to his use of steroids and other performance-enhancing substances.

Said, who is not a medical expert and uses some performance-enhancing drugs, has defended their use in controlled and managed settings.

"I think they definitely have their place in competitive sports, in bodybuilding, and in recovery," he said.

The ABC has reported not only on the booming unregulated trade of peptides, but also the severe health complications they can pose.

There are also medical concerns about the illicit trade of peptides and separately the side-effects of prescribed peptides.

It is a particularly pertinent question for the legacy of a man whose image has become synonymous with the pursuit of the perfect physique, and a confronting detail in a story that has otherwise been relentlessly mythologised, because Zyzz became something larger than the person his brother remembers.

"To me, I always would see him as my younger, goofy, dorky, highly intellectual brother," said Said.

He understands why people still idolise Zyzz, but is less comfortable with the comparisons that have turned his brother into a larger-than-life figure.

"Az was just as much human as you and I," he said.

Reflecting on Zyzz's life, Said explained that his flaws are what made him relatable.

"Why does a role model always have to be completely virtuous?" Said asked.

Aziz, he argued, was "imperfectly perfect".

A young man with faults, ambitions and insecurities who happened to become extraordinarily good at making people watch him.

World.title: Chinese robot beats Usain Bolt's 100m world record
World.content:
A Chinese humanoid robot ran 100 metres in 9.39 seconds in a preliminary heat at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday, faster than the men's world record held by Jamaican sprinting great Usain Bolt.

Tiangong Ultra, developed by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, won its heat at the opening of the games' second edition, organisers said.

The robot overtook smartphone maker Honor's Lightning near the finish after falling behind early in the race. Lightning finished in 9.47 seconds, also faster than the 9.58-second record Bolt set at the 2009 World Athletics Championships in Berlin.

The results marked a sharp improvement from last year's inaugural games, when Tiangong Ultra won the 100m in 21.50 seconds. Tiangong also won the world's first humanoid robot half-marathon, held in Beijing last year.

Humanoid robots compete during a 400m preliminary race, following the opening ceremony of the 2026 World Humanoid Robot Games. (Reuters: Tingshu Wang)

Earlier on Saturday, Chinese state media reported that Lightning had run 100m in 9.32 seconds in a preparatory test, reaching a peak speed of 14.5m per second.

Lightning won this year's humanoid half-marathon in 50 minutes and 26 seconds, faster than the pace of the elite men's human world record.

Lightning stood 169cm tall and had 95-cm legs during the half-marathon. Its researchers later lengthened its legs by 10cm ahead of the games, according to broadcaster CCTV.

The 100m is among 51 events at the games, which include football, dancing and industrial-task contests.

The 'Robot Olympics'

This year's World Humanoid Robot Games opened on Saturday. (Reuters: Florence Lo)

It's been called the Robot Olympics. But unlike the human Olympics, Team China is collecting almost all the medals.

Running from August 22 to 26, this year's World Humanoid Robot Games mark the second edition of the latest and biggest incarnation of China's robot games, which have been taking place for the past decade.

The 2026 games add a challenge for robotic hands, with robots judged on their speed and accuracy in precision tasks: tightening screws, opening bottles and picking up beads with tweezers.

The shift to work tasks in the games reflects the increasingly crowded industry's biggest problem: showing prototypes can work in the real world.

Robotic competitions in China have provided a window into the advances of a now surging sector — and the importance of its success as a strategic industry singled out by President Xi Jinping.

Once a curiosity organised by academic teams and hobbyists, China's robot games have become a national showcase celebrated by state media — and, increasingly, a proving ground for commercial products from companies looking to show real-world applications beyond the spectacle.

China has been promoting humanoid robots as a strategic emerging industry, with policymakers and companies betting that advances in AI and hardware will accelerate their deployment in manufacturing, logistics and consumer applications.

Reuters

World.title: World boxing champion shot dead outside his home in South Africa
World.content:
Former world boxing champion Zolani "Last Born" Tete has been shot dead outside his home in South Africa's Eastern Cape province, police and the country's sports minister said.

The 38-year-old was arriving at his residence in Mdantsane township when two armed men wearing balaclavas got out of a vehicle and opened fire.

"I will not speculate about who did this or why," Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie said in a statement.

Tete's killing will renew attention on violent crime in South Africa, which continues to have one of the world's highest murder rates despite recent declines in homicides.

The killing was condemned by Eastern Cape Premier Oscar Mabunyane. (Reuters)

The murder of the world champion has also struck a chord in Mdantsane, the Eastern Cape township that has produced some of South Africa's most successful boxers.

SABC, the South African public broadcaster, reported that Eastern Cape Premier Oscar Mabuyane expressed shock and sadness at Tete's killing.

A spokesperson for the premier said: "It is heartbreaking that a life that brought so much pride to our province has been ended through such a brutal act of violence," according to SABC.

"We call on law enforcement agencies to leave no stone unturned to establish what happened and bring those responsible to book. Anyone with information must assist the police.

"On behalf of Premier Mabuyane and the EC provincial government, we extend our deepest condolences to the Tete family, his friends, the boxing fraternity and the community of Mdantsane.”

A woman travelling with Zolani Tete was also shot during the attack. (Reuters)

A 27-year-old woman travelling with Tete was shot multiple times and taken to hospital. Police have started investigations and the motive remains unclear.

Tete won the IBF junior bantamweight world title in 2014 after defeating Japan's Teiru Kinoshita in Kobe. He later won the WBO bantamweight crown.

He tested positive for the steroid stanozolol after a fight against British boxer Jason Cunningham in 2022 and was given a four-year suspension from competing, which expired in July this year.

He is best remembered internationally for his 11-second knockout of fellow South African Siboniso Gonya in Belfast in November 2017, the fastest stoppage in a world title fight.

Reuters

World.title: Mackay makes cricket history as day one of inaugural Test match sells out
World.content:
Barry Jansen mortgaged his house to help buy land for a cricket arena and didn't tell his wife for five years.

More than 40 years later, history is being made on the same field as the Queensland city of Mackay hosts its first international Test cricket match.

Mr Jansen said in the late 1980s the cricket association wanted to expand but needed financial backing.

Three members took an extraordinary personal risk and mortgaged their homes to help make it happen.

"We couldn't afford to pay our groundsmen without extending our facility. We didn't have the finance. We had park land with some value and that was all," he said.

Mackay cricket stalwart Barry Jansen in the commentary box. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

A government grant and a bank loan guaranteed by three members' homes helped fund the expansion.

Mr Jansen said there were a "couple of quiet moments" about five years later when he told his wife he'd mortgaged their home.

"I was very, very fortunate. I always say, it [Harrup Park] is like one of the family," he said.

"My wife always says it was part of the family because we'd sunk so much in it."

Nicolas Jones and Joe Brayshaw are on safari from Brisbane for the test. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

In 1939 the field was a cow paddock, purchased by local farmers for 1,000 pounds to start a cricket club.

"It was definitely a risk but those people then created the vision and we had to do it," Mr Jansen said.

'True cricket lovers'

Grandstands and hills at Harrup Park's Great Barrier Reef Arena were packed out with Bangladeshi locals waving flags and placards, with a "tiger" or two in the mix.

Shagufta Hasan, who described herself as a "true cricket lover", said Mackay's Bangladeshi community was cricket obsessed.

Members of Mackay's Bangladeshi community were out in force to support their team. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

"It doesn't matter if Bangladesh are playing or not, we're always watching," she said.

"We have 32 Bangladeshi families in Mackay so when the news came we all are very excited."

Scoring dream

Mackay resident Mel Dwyer, one of two Cricket Australia official scorers at the game, said it was a dream come true to score a Test in her home town.

She made her Test scoring debut at the Gabba in 2024 for Australia vs West Indies.

Mel Dwyer says scoring a Test match in her home town of Mackay was a dream come true. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

Matches are scored on paper and she said the slower pace of a Test made the job "a little bit easier" than a T20 match.

"There are plenty of sets of eyes watching and there's lots of talking going on as far as what happens with every ball. We have to confirm everything," she said.

Ms Dwyer started scoring about 12 years ago when her youngest child started playing representative cricket.

"I just put my hand up to help out with those games because I found that if I sat on the sideline with the other parents, I would be too engrossed in conversations with them and miss what was actually going on the field," she said.

Cricket fans from Sydney flew in for the test match. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

Ms Dwyer grew up in a family of cricket lovers in a house full of memorabilia celebrating Sir Donald Bradman and the Invincibles.

"I never thought in my wildest dreams that I would be working in cricket and scoring Test matches. A five-day test match would be absolutely amazing," she said.

Strong pitch

Peter Kazakoff, head curator of Great Barrier Reef Arena, said perfect weather and just the right amount of rain earlier in the week combined for a strong pitch.

The wicket in Mackay has the same clay soil profile as the Gabba.

"We source it from the same paddock down in Peak Crossing just at the back of Ipswich," he said.

Mr Kazakoff said selectors, coaches and players had been "blown out of the water" by the playing surface.

"We've gone from being a country cricket ground to an international test cricket venue. It's quite remarkable."

World.title: Quick hits: Stunning Shoriful rivals Starc's staggering spell, Hazlewood fumes
World.content:
Two lethal left arm quicks combine for 12 wickets, Australia comes close to snaring the rarest of dismissals, and a Harrup Park specialist fails on his return to the team.

Here are the quick hits from day one of the second Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

1. Sensational Starc's first-ball strike

Mitchell Starc claimed a first ball wicket in both of this first two overs. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

We've seen this play before: Four times, in fact.

Mitch Starc steaming in, an opening batter studiously preparing for a lengthy stay at the crease, only to succumb to the very first challenge.

Shadman Islam was the unfortunate batter on this occasion, looking to clip Starc into the leg side but misjudging the pace and sending a leading edge to Cameron Green at gully.

He is, incredibly, the fourth batter to fall to Starc with the very first ball of a Test match.

Sri Lankan opener Dimuth Karunaratne was his first such victim back in 2016.

England's Rory Burns was famously bowled around his legs at the Gabba in the 2021/22 Ashes series.

And then, in 2024 at Adelaide Oval, Yashavi Jaiswal was trapped LBW with a pink ball.

Oh, and he wasn't done there, either.

2. Starc's five-fa comes in just 22 balls

Mitchell Starc tore through the top order. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Mitch Starc would not be contained or limited with just one wicket in his first spell.

Incredibly, he took five, tearing through the Bangladesh top order like a cyclone of ill-intent.

Shadman Islam's wicket was the only one to fall in the first over.

But in his second, he took two in the first two balls, accounting for Tanzid and Shanto in consecutive balls.

Mominul survived the first ball of the third over, but shouldn't have let down his guard as he fell later in the very same over to make it 4 in 3 for the big left-hander.

And then, in his fourth over, he made it five, Litton Das falling LBW for yet another duck, his five wickets coming in just 22 balls.

It should have been just 21 balls, had Beau Webster not shelled the sort of ball that you'd toss up to a toddler in the backyard.

It didn't matter though, Starc could not be contained, ending his six-over spell with figures of 5-5 and four maidens, leaving Bangladesh 5-15.

It was the sixth fastest five-wicket haul in Test history, but remarkably, it wasn't Starc's fastest in the format — that came in just 15 balls against the West Indies last year.

3. Obstructing the field?

Hazlewood was unimpressed with Taskin. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Fans of obscure dismissals were almost gifted a rare instance of a player obstructing the field in the later stages of Bangladesh's batting innings.

Hazlewood came in and Taskin swiped across the line, sending the ball straight up in the air.

Hazlewood raced towards the ball, as Taskin took off for a run, before he then realised Hazlewood was baring down on him.

Taskin attempted to cover up, Hazlewood barged into him and the ball fell safe.

The crowd in Mackay felt aggrieved and there was more than a small suggestion of obstructing the field.

Hazlewood's eyes were in danger of having to be registered as dangerous weapons such was the ferocity of the daggers he was giving the unfortunate batter, as Pat Cummins engaged in a discussion with umpire Nitin Menon.

There was no appeal though that we could see, and Taskin was reprieved.

Only one player has ever been given out obstructing the field in Test cricket, Len Hutton for England against South Africa at The Oval in 1951.

Incredibly, later in the over, it appeared there was an (inadvertent) case of a double hit too as an attempted pull shot went awry.

4. Renshaw out cheaply on Test return

Renshaw was dimissed cheaply on his return to the Test arena. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

If Matt Renshaw could have chosen any ground in the world to make his Test return, it may well have been Harrup Park.

The Queenslander is the leading First Class run scorer at the venue, and is the only man to have scored two Sheffield Shield centuries in Mackay.

He's also coming off an impressive domestic summer, during which he scored three red-ball centuries at an average flirting with 50.

And it was under porcelain blue skies and in what looked to be perfect batting conditions that he made his way back to the Test-match crease, with the pitch having flattened out since Starc's new-ball demolition job.

The southpaw made an assured start to his innings, working a few attractive runs through the off-side, but it wasn't long before he was back in the sheds, having edged one into the slips.

Renshaw was out for 8 and Bangladesh, in desperate need of an early wicket after being bundled out for just 64, had their breakthrough.

5. Shoriful's dream day

The towering Shoriful made an instant impact at the bowling crease. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Forced to sit out the first Test with a side strain, exciting fast bowler Shoriful Islam wasted no time in making an impact in Mackay.

The 25-year-old left-armer is just that little bit quicker than his more workmanlike pace-bowling colleagues, and at over 190 centimetres tall, provides a different challenge in terms of release point.

Coming into the attack at first change, Shoriful took just two deliveries to claim his first Test wicket in Australia.

Pitching on a good length and seaming into Travis Head, the Australian opener was caught trying to play a shot that was never there, and was out chopping on for the third innings in a row.

Three balls later, and Shoriful had his second.

This time, he was aided by thigh pad rather than willow, with the ball rolling onto the stumps after thudding into Marnus Labuschagne.

Labuschagne was in disbelief, Shoriful was in dreamland, and Bangladesh was making a fist of things in Mackay.

And the towering left-armer wasn't done there.

First, he produced a beauty to dismiss Smith, who was well set on 42, LBW midway through the evening session.

Then, he tore through the Australian lower order, conjuring three more moments of magic to dismiss Beau Webster and Cummins for ducks, and Starc for 1.

World.title: Pendlebury could miss rest of season with his playing future undecided
World.content:
Scott Pendlebury's glittering Collingwood career could be over after the AFL/VFL games record holder suffered a hamstring injury.

The 38-year-old will miss up to three weeks, ruling him out of at least next week's historic wildcard match.

In an added blow for the Magpies, tough defender Brayden Maynard suffered a knee injury at training and is in doubt to return this season, no matter how far Collingwood progress in finals.

"These are obviously disappointing setbacks for both Scott and Brayden," Collingwood football boss Charlie Gardiner said.

"These are unfortunate setbacks especially at this time of year, but Scott and Brayden are absolute professionals and will do all they can to get back as quickly as possible."

Pendlebury was ruled out in the second quarter of Friday night's 63-point thrashing by Brisbane at the MCG with what Collingwood described as a "knee bursa".

But scans on Saturday revealed a hamstring strain that will sideline him for two or three weeks.

It comes at a critical time for the 21-season veteran, who is waiting until the end of the year to decide if he plays on in 2027.

McKenna, Morris magic lifts Lions to vital big win over Pies Brisbane Lions put the foot down against Collingwood, with magic from Conor McKenna and Logan Morris seeing the premiers take a strong grip on third spot.

If he does not retire, Pendlebury has also received an offer from Gold Coast to be effectively an on-field playing coach next year.

Collingwood are carefully balancing how they deal with an iconic player contemplating his football mortality.

Pendlebury was also substituted four-and-a-half minutes into last year's preliminary-final loss to Brisbane with calf tightness.

Collingwood would likely err on the side of caution, desperate to avoid a repeat, even if the Magpies are still in premiership contention when he is available.

The Magpies would have to play five straight weeks of knockout finals to claim the most unlikely of premierships.

"That'll all be weighed up," coach Craig McRae said.

"He (Maynard) might be right to go, but then do we want to take that risk?"

The Magpies were conservative with Isaac Quaynor, Patrick Lipinski and Maynard on Friday night.

All three were expected to return next week, but Maynard is now no chance.

"Brayden unfortunately left the track early this morning during a training session, with scans confirming he sustained a grade-one MCL strain," Gardiner said.

"This is the same knee but unrelated to his earlier injury."

Collingwood also managed the game time of Nick Daicos and Darcy Cameron against the Lions in anticipation of the wildcard game, which McRae insisted felt like a final.

AAP

Tech.title: Doodle generative compositions in your browser with Musical Spirograph
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

I remember having a Spirograph as a kid and being obsessed with it. Its geometric patterns are hypnotic and gorgeous. I also love generative music composition. So bringing those two things together in a browser tab, I’m hooked. Musical Spirograph is a relatively simple concept. A set of points dash around the screen according to mathematical equations, generating hypotrochoids and epitrochoids. Those points pass through a series of concentric rings which trigger specific notes.

Honestly, that alone is fun enough, but you can customize it quite a bit. There are six different virtual rotors to pick from, you can have up to three arms drawing simultaneously, and there are a bunch of other parameters to tweak the pattern. Then there are six different scale options, or you can completely customize the notes, and there are six different synth presets. Plus you can change the quantization and BPM, or even expand the number of rings out to two octaves.

Sure, the sound engine isn’t great, and it’s prone to clipping and artifacts. And I really wish there was a way to get MIDI out of it to control other instruments. But it’s still a ton of fun to get lost in for a while.

Tech.title: W. Kamau Bell has the most practical ‘most indispensable tool’
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

W. Kamau Bell is one of those people who has always just seemed to be there. From Totally Biased, to Politically Re-Active, United Shades of America, and We Need to Talk About Cosby, his blend of comedy, social commentary, and political activism has helped him stand out. He’s won a Peabody and four Emmys, been a Celebrity Jeopardy! champion, received honors from the ACLU, and been crowned the Ambassador of Fishbone by founding member Chris Dowd. Bell is, if nothing else, a busy man.

So we’re very grateful that he took time between episodes of his podcast Who’s With Me, his comedy tour, and Substack of the same name, promoting his upcoming children’s book Rock Paper Scissors Cheese (out October 27th), and, of course, being a dad, to answer our weekly questionnaire.

What is your most indispensable tool?

A charger. All of this is just shiny paperweights without a charger.

Which app is the most underappreciated?

I probably use the map app every day. I wish MapQuest’s app was better, so I didn’t have to use the Trump Billionaire guys’ apps. You know who I’m talking about. The map apps that have the Gulf of Mexico listed as the Gulf of America. SOOOOOOOOO EMBARRASSING!!!

What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?

It’s been a long, loooong time since I had a phone that didn’t just transfer my old apps over, but I would guess that if I had a clean phone with only the basic apps on it, I would quickly install YouTube. What do you expect me to do? Just think my own thoughts all day? I need somebody constantly telling me something about something. Or singing me something about something.

What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?

Just come in a hard case with that piece of plastic that claims it stops your screen from cracking already on the phone. I just bought it. I don’t need a project, and I’m not comfortable asking the person at the cellphone place to do it for me. Also, I’m sure it is a scam, but I just put it on there anyway.

How many tabs do you have open right now?

I have 17 windows open across two different browser windows. That’s light work. When I’m writing a Substack article, I can get to 30 windows… easy. I only close them when I hit “publish” on an article. I have to earn the right to close a window.

Which social media platform do you use the most (if any)?

I really want to thank Elon Musk for breaking my addiction to Twitter. It wasn’t healthy, so I can say that he really improved my life by ruining Twitter. These days, I’m an Instagram and Threads guy. Not that Zuckerberg is significantly better than Elon, but as a public-facing person, I do need these platforms. But Zuckerberg better be careful. My generation isn’t afraid to leave social media platforms. We left MySpace and Friendster, just like I left Twitter.

What is your happy place online?

Watching the latest Japanese video on YouTube or watching Lionfield videos with my 8-year-old on Instagram

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

Afro pick with extra-long metal teeth with a fist as the handle.

Which was the most disappointing?

A brush that claimed it could effectively comb Afros. I bought it because of Shark Tank. But I think my hair is just too long. Or the X-ray specs they used to sell in comic books.

What game do you have the fondest memories of?

It is a tie between Civilization on the PC and NBA Live on Sega Genesis. I’m talking like NBA Live ‘95. I’M SOOOOO OLD!

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

AI.

What is one thing you wish you had created?

Flappy Bird. But I would have let it rock instead of deleting it. Maybe because I have three kids, I can’t look a gift app in the mouth like that. You all would have had at least eight Flappy Bird movies by now. It would have out-Minioned the Minion movies.

What creation are you most proud of?

My three daughters. It was a collab project.

What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?

“Don’t think you are going to make it just by doing stand-up comedy. You need to learn how to write other things,” – Kevin Kataoka.

What is your current obsession?

The NBA off-season. It is way better than the actual season, even with the Knicks winning.

What do you do when you need to focus?

Coffee and extreme quiet… like leave me the eff alone… so I can listen to YouTube while I work. Middle of the night is the best time to work, but I can’t do that as often as I like… those three kids like it when both their parents are awake at the same time. My wife likes that better, too.

What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?

Change the song or play a silly cellphone game for four hours. Do you know YouTube has games now for free???

When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?

Excuse me? EXCUSE ME??? WHY WOULD I DO THAT?

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

I’m a middle-aged-dad-who-buys-records-years-old. The guy at the shop (Mars Records in Oakland) holds things for me. I bought Fishbone’s first EP recently. I should really buy a record player.

What do you think is worth splurging on?

If you need a new computer, GET A NEW COMPUTER!

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

Doing the best he can.

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

Tech.title: Amazon just hiked the prices for Echo, Fire TV, and Kindle products by up to 60 percent
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Citing “significant increases in memory and storage component costs,” Amazon has raised prices on Echos, Kindles, Fire TVs, and Eeros by up to 60 percent, as first reported by Fortune.

The cheapest products in Amazon’s lineup were hit hardest, with the Echo Dot smart speaker jumping from $49.99 to $79.99. The Fire TV Stick 4K Max also rose by over 40 percent to $84.99, and the base level Kindle now costs $149.99, a nearly 37 percent increase.

In a statement to The Verge, Kristy Schmidt, senior communications manager of Amazon’s Devices & Services divison, said, “The consumer electronics industry is facing significant increases in memory and storage component costs. After absorbing these increases for as long as we could, we recently adjusted pricing across our product lines. Our approach has always been to offer great products at accessible prices, and that commitment hasn’t changed.”

Amazon’s flagship Echo Dot Max smart speaker, which launched last year, now costs $119.99, up from $99.99. Apple increased the price of its comparable HomePod Mini this summer to $129 from $99.99, also in response to rising costs. The Google Home Speaker remains at $99.99 for now.

Amazon hardware products apparently not affected include its line of Ring cameras and video doorbells, and the Echo Studio, its higher-end $219.99 smart speaker.

Tech.title: An okay laptop with 16GB of RAM is better than a nice laptop with 8GB, and this $520 HP OmniBook proves it
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

Laptop prices are out of whack. $500 used to get you a tolerable laptop, and $900 got you a really good one. They often had similar CPU, RAM, and storage options because that stuff was comparatively cheap; the difference was often in build quality and screen rather than power. But RAMageddon has thrown everything off. Even laptops like the $950 Surface Laptop now start with 8GB of RAM, which isn’t enough. And on the lower end, where manufacturers are struggling to compete with the $700 MacBook Neo, they’re cutting corners on storage, CPU, and build quality too.

However, one low-cost laptop has bucked this and genuinely surprised me. HP’s 16-inch OmniBook 3 is a basic productivity laptop that regularly goes for around $520 at Walmart and Amazon. It has Qualcomm’s base Snapdragon X chip, meaning passable everyday performance and excellent battery life. But it also has a humdrum screen, mediocre speakers, a run-of-the-mill trackpad, and a plastic build. Pre-RAMageddon, it would be nothing to write home about.

But 16GB of RAM and a 512GB SSD in an okay laptop for around $500? That counts as good news in 2026.

The entry-level OmniBook 3 I tested has an 8-core Snapdragon X processor, 16GB of RAM, 512GB SSD, and a 16-inch 1920 x 1200 anti-glare IPS LCD. And the OmniBook 3 is fairly portable for a larger laptop with lots of ports. It’s barely heavier than a 14-inch MacBook Pro, and at a maximum thickness of 0.63 inches / 16mm it’s decently thin. This big laptop doesn’t feel big. And despite a plastic chassis and low price it doesn’t feel too cheap either.

Component report card Screen: D

Webcam: C

Keyboard: C

Trackpad: C

Port selection: B

Speakers: D

Number of ugly stickers to remove: 2

As much as I would like to see more cheap Windows laptops with the sleek looks and sturdy all-metal build of the MacBook Neo, I wouldn’t mind if more of them were like the OmniBook 3. Its screen, keyboard, trackpad, and webcam are all at least passable to decent. There isn’t anything special here, but unlike the Chuwi UniBook there’s also nothing that feels like a punishment.

The 1920 x 1200 / 60Hz screen isn’t high-quality or bright enough to combat the sun when taken outside (it maxes out at 300 nits of brightness and covers a paltry 62.5 percent of the sRGB color space), but it isn’t washed out or bleeding light at its edges. The mechanical trackpad has a basic diving board-style hinge, but a confident and decent-feeling kachunk-y click. The 1080p webcam is actually fairly sharp, and it does a good job handling backlight from a bright window — with only a hint of green color cast. But hey, at least it has Windows Hello face unlocking. And at least this not-too-large large laptop has lots of ports and charges via USB-C with a very compact 65W GaN charger.

Just one USB-A and an audio jack on this side. But another USB-A, two USB-C, and HDMI over here. The left-aligned keyboard and trackpad allow for a generously sized numpad.

My biggest gripe is the dual speakers (unsurprisingly), which lack bass and sound too treble-y, but they’re just tolerable enough to live with. My next biggest is the keyboard (surprisingly). I usually like HP keyboards, but this one feels too stiff. If you’re the type to hammer your fingers down and you love a generously sized number pad you might be fine, but I get more typos than I’m used to from keys not registering. I could learn to live with it, but I’d still prefer not to have to.

HP OmniBook 3 16 / Qualcomm Snapdragon X X1-26-100 / 16GB / 512GB MacBook Neo / Apple A18 Pro / 8GB / 256GB Chuwi UniBook / Intel Core 3 304 “Wildcat Lake” / 8GB / 256GB Microsoft Surface Laptop 13-inch (2026) / Qualcomm Snapdragon X Plus X1P-46-100 / 8GB / 256GB Acer Aspire 14 AI / Intel Core Ultra 7 256V / 16GB / 1TB Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3x / Qualcomm Snapdragon X X1-26-100 / 16GB / 256GB CPU cores 8 6 5 8 8 8 GPU Adreno X1-45 A18 Pro (5 GPU cores) Intel Graphics (1 GPU core) Adreno X1-45 Intel Arc 140V (8 GPU cores) Adreno X1-45 Geekbench 6 CPU Single 2142 3402 2385 2348 2769 2137 Geekbench 6 CPU Multi 10593 8508 6187 9421 10930 9728 Geekbench 6 GPU (OpenCL) 9577 19798 6019 9554 28556 9689 Premiere 4K Export (lower is better) 12 minutes, 8 seconds 8 minutes, 30 seconds 1 hour, 9 minutes, 29 seconds Crashed 7 minutes, 28 seconds 12 minutes, 59 seconds Sustained SSD reads (MB/s) 5017.12 1735.91 2394.57 3804.31 6391.51 5738.86 Sustained SSD writes (MB/s) 4370.35 1684.05 2092.66 3310.94 5524.22 2801.02 Price as tested about $520 $699 $449 $949.99 $1,049.99 $749.99

What I can totally live with is the performance. The OmniBook’s 8-core Snapdragon X processor is a little slower than the one in the $950 Surface Laptop I tested, but the OmniBook’s day-to-day performance is better because it’s not starved for RAM and its larger SSD is a little faster. Like other lower-end Snapdragon laptop chips it’s not going to wow you with graphics performance or tackle heavy content creation in Adobe apps, but it’s perfectly adequate for everyday multitasking work. Even when running several apps with a couple dozen Chrome tabs left open, including a video podcast playing, I didn’t feel it slow down the way the Surface Laptop or Chuwi UniBook, each with only 8GB of RAM, did.

And while a Snapdragon chip means this Windows laptop isn’t ideal for gaming, it does make it great on battery. You can pretty easily get around 12 hours of mixed web usage with a bit of music or video streaming.

It feels like the money went into the core specs of the OmniBook 3, and HP just barely stuck the landing on the right compromises elsewhere. As much as I adore the build quality of Microsoft’s Surface Laptops, if I were spending my own money I’d choose the OmniBook 3, never worry about how much RAM is in use, and save over $400.

Previous Next













1 / 8 The screen is bright enough to use it near a big window, but outside it’s difficult to see even in the shade.

If we reviewed the OmniBook 3 a year ago I might feel different, but it’s been a tiny breath of fresh air to use something this cheap and mostly think, “Not too bad!” Especially coming right after I tested the $450 Chuwi UniBook. An employee being issued this laptop for work shouldn’t feel like their IT department totally hates them. And while I think a MacBook Neo would still be a better all-around experience for a school-age kid, I’d totally understand saving nearly $200 to get the OmniBook 3 if a budget can’t be stretched.

My only worry is that the OmniBook 3’s price will go up like everything else. While there are more sub-$800 laptops coming, and I’ll be testing more very soon, the OmniBook 3’s price — and that of the OmniBook 5 I reviewed back in December — feel anomalous right now. The RAMageddon storm could eventually ruin them like it did many other laptops and devices. But, for now, there’s some safe harbor with this lowly OmniBook.
